data.title: focus
data.summary: Lesson 11 reviews the main ideas of calculus and shows how limits, derivatives, and integrals work together to solve real‑world problems. Students will practice linking these tools across physics, biology, and economics contexts.
objectives: Identify how limits, derivatives, and integrals are connected
Apply each calculus tool to a simple physics, biology, or economics scenario
Explain why choosing the right tool matters for a given problem
Solve a multi‑step problem that uses a limit, a derivative, and an integral
Reflect on the solution process to build confidence in using calculus
data.prerequisites: Students should already know basic limits, derivative rules, and antiderivative techniques from earlier lessons.
why: Calculus is the language of change. Engineers use limits to predict system behavior, biologists model population growth with derivatives, and economists evaluate profit trends with integrals. Understanding how these tools fit together lets you choose the right method for any situation.

Real‑world problems rarely stay within one calculus topic. By mastering the connections, you can tackle complex tasks—like finding the speed of a car, the rate of drug absorption, or the total cost of production—more efficiently and with greater confidence.

sections.heading: 1. Review of Core Concepts
sections.body:
Recall that a **limit** tells us what value a function $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to as the input $x$ approaches a particular point $a$.  
We write this as  

$$\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L,$$  

meaning “as $x$ gets nearer and nearer to $a$, the outputs $f(x)$ get nearer and nearer to $L$.”  
Think of a car approaching a stop sign: the car’s speed may never actually become zero until it stops, but we can describe the speed it is *approaching* as it gets closer to the sign. The limit captures that “approaching” idea without requiring the function to actually reach the value at $a$.

> **Definition:** A limit $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L$ exists if we can make $f(x)$ as close as we wish to $L$ by choosing $x$ sufficiently close (but not equal) to $a$.

The **derivative** measures how fast a function changes at a single point. Formally, it is the limit of the average rate of change over a shrinking interval:

$$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.$$

Here $h$ is a tiny step away from $a$, and the fraction $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ is the slope of the secant line joining $(a,f(a))$ and $(a+h,f(a+h))$. As $h$ shrinks, the secant line tilts toward the **tangent line**, the straight line that just touches the curve at $(a,f(a))$ without crossing it. The slope of this tangent line is the derivative $f'(a)$.

> **In daily life:** If $f(t)$ gives the distance a runner has traveled after $t$ minutes, then $f'(t)$ is the runner’s instantaneous speed at that exact minute—how fast the distance is changing right then.

An **antiderivative** (also called an indefinite integral) works in the opposite direction. It is a function $F(x)$ whose derivative returns the original function $f(x)$:

$$F'(x)=f(x).$$

Because adding a constant $C$ does not change the derivative, every antiderivative comes in a family $F(x)+C$. Geometrically, $F(x)$ can be thought of as the “area under the curve” of $f$ measured from a fixed starting point, though that interpretation becomes precise when we move to definite integrals later.

> **Note:** The antiderivative is not a single function but a whole set of functions that differ only by a constant.

Why are these ideas useful together? The limit gives us a rigorous way to talk about “instantaneous” behavior, which the derivative captures as a single number—the slope of the tangent. The antiderivative then tells us how to reconstruct the original function from its slopes. This three‑part relationship—limit → derivative → antiderivative—forms the backbone of calculus.

Consider a simple parabola $f(x)=x^{2}$. Its limit as $x$ approaches $3$ is $\lim_{x\to3}x^{2}=9$. Using the definition of the derivative,

$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(x+h)^{2}-x^{2}}{h}
       =\lim_{h\to0}\frac{2xh+h^{2}}{h}
       =\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h)=2x,$$

so at $x=3$ the slope of the tangent line is $f'(3)=6$. An antiderivative of $f$ is $F(x)=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C$, because differentiating $F$ gives back $x^{2}$.

> **Remember:** A limit describes a value we get *close to*; a derivative is the *instantaneous rate of change* found by a limit; an antiderivative is a function whose *derivative brings us back* to the original.

Keeping these geometric pictures in mind—approaching a point, a tangent line touching a curve, and a curve built up from tiny sloping pieces—will help you see how limits, derivatives, and antiderivatives fit together as tools for describing change.

sections.heading: 2. The Relationship Between Limits and Derivatives
sections.body:
When we talk about a **derivative**, we are really asking one question: *How fast is something changing at this exact instant?*  
To answer that, we look at the change over a very short time interval, then let that interval become *as small as possible*. The tool that lets us do this is the **limit**.

> **Definition:** The derivative of a function $f$ at a point $x=a$ is the limit of the difference quotient  
> $$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.$$

The expression inside the limit, $\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$, is called the **difference quotient**. It measures the average rate of change of $f$ over the interval from $a$ to $a+h$. Think of $h$ as a tiny step forward on the $x$‑axis. The numerator $f(a+h)-f(a)$ tells us how much the function’s value rises (or falls) during that step, and dividing by $h$ spreads that change out over the length of the step, giving an average slope.

Why do we let $h$ go to zero? Imagine you are driving and you want to know your speed at a particular instant, not just the average speed over a mile. If you look at your odometer after a long stretch, you get an average speed. To get the instantaneous speed, you would need to look at the distance covered in an *infinitesimally* short time. The limit does exactly that: it shrinks the interval until the average slope becomes the true slope at the single point.

### Step‑by‑step example

Let’s find the derivative of the simple function $f(x)=x^{2}$ at the point $x=3$.

1. **Write the difference quotient.**  
   $$\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h} = \frac{(3+h)^{2}-3^{2}}{h}.$$

2. **Expand the numerator.**  
   $(3+h)^{2}=9+6h+h^{2}$, so  
   $$\frac{9+6h+h^{2}-9}{h}= \frac{6h+h^{2}}{h}.$$

3. **Factor out $h$ from the numerator.**  
   $$\frac{h(6+h)}{h}.$$

4. **Cancel the common factor $h$ (provided $h\neq0$).**  
   $$6+h.$$

5. **Take the limit as $h\to0$.**  
   $$\lim_{h\to0}(6+h)=6.$$

Thus $f'(3)=6$. In words, the slope of the parabola $y=x^{2}$ at $x=3$ is $6$; the function is increasing six units in $y$ for each one unit you move to the right in $x$ at that exact spot.

> **In daily life:** If you picture a hill shaped like $y=x^{2}$, the derivative at a point tells you how steep the hill feels right under your feet. Standing at $x=3$, the hill feels as steep as a slope of $6$ (rise $6$ meters for every meter you walk forward).

> **Note:** The limit only exists if the left‑hand and right‑hand approaches give the same number. If they differ, the function has no derivative there (a corner or cusp).

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to cancel the $h$ before taking the limit. If you try to plug $h=0$ directly into $\frac{6h+h^{2}}{h}$ you get $\frac{0}{0}$, an undefined expression. Cancelling first simplifies the fraction so the limit can be evaluated.

### Why this matters

Knowing that a derivative is a limit of a difference quotient connects two core ideas of calculus: **limits** (the language of approaching) and **rates of change** (the language of derivatives). This bridge lets us move from geometric notions of slope to algebraic formulas we can compute, and later to the reverse process—integrals—where we add up infinitely many tiny pieces.

> **Remember:** The derivative $f'(a)$ is *the* limit of the average slope as the interval shrinks to zero. It gives the exact instantaneous rate of change at $x=a$.

sections.heading: 3. From Derivatives to Integrals
sections.body:
When we first met derivatives, we thought of them as “instantaneous rates of change.”  
If $f(t)$ tells us the position of a car at time $t$, then $f'(t)$ tells us the car’s speed at that exact moment.  

Now imagine we know the speed function $v(t)=f'(t)$ and we want to recover the original position $f(t)$.  
The **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC)** tells us exactly how to do that: it says that integration, the process of adding up tiny pieces, is the inverse operation of differentiation.

> **Definition:** *Fundamental Theorem of Calculus* –  
> If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $F$ is any function whose derivative is $f$ (that is, $F'(x)=f(x)$), then  
> $$\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a).$$  

In words, the total accumulated change of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ equals the difference between the values of an antiderivative $F$ at the endpoints.  

Why does this work? Think of the interval $[a,b]$ as a road. The derivative $f(x)$ tells us the slope of the road at each point – how steep it is. If we slice the road into many tiny pieces of length $\Delta x$, the change in height over each piece is approximately $f(x_i)\,\Delta x$. Adding all those little changes gives an estimate of the total height gain. When we let the pieces become infinitely small, the sum becomes the integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, and the exact total change is captured by $F(b)-F(a)$.  

> **In daily life:** Imagine filling a bathtub. The water flow rate $r(t)$ (liters per minute) is like a derivative. The amount of water that has entered after $t$ minutes is the integral $\int_0^{t} r(s)\,ds$. The FTC tells us that if we know a function $R(t)$ whose rate of change is $r(t)$, then the water volume at time $t$ is simply $R(t)-R(0)$.  

The theorem has two parts. The first part guarantees that the integral of a continuous function produces an antiderivative. The second part, the formula shown above, lets us evaluate a definite integral by finding any antiderivative $F$. This is why we often write  

$$\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \bigl[\,F(x)\,\bigr]_{a}^{b} = F(b)-F(a).$$  

Here the brackets $[\,\,]_{a}^{b}$ remind us to plug in the upper limit $b$ and subtract the value at the lower limit $a$.

> **Note:** The function $F$ does not have to be the *only* antiderivative; any one works because any two antiderivatives differ by a constant, and that constant cancels when we compute $F(b)-F(a)$.  

Understanding the FTC gives us a powerful bridge:  

* From a **rate** (derivative) we can find the **total amount** (integral).  
* From a **total amount** we can recover the **average rate** by dividing by the interval length:  
  $$\text{average rate} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx.$$  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to add the “$+C$” when finding an antiderivative for an *indefinite* integral, and then using that incomplete $F$ in the FTC formula. The constant cancels in a definite integral, but you must still write it when solving for $F$ first.  

Because the FTC links differentiation and integration, we can choose the tool that best matches the problem. If a problem gives us a rate and asks for total change, we integrate. If it gives us a total change and asks for the rate at a point, we differentiate.  

> **Remember:** The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus tells us that *adding up tiny changes* (integration) exactly reverses *measuring an instant’s change* (differentiation). This symmetry is the heart of calculus and will appear again whenever we move between motion, growth, area, or any situation where rates and totals interact.

sections.heading: 4. Choosing the Right Tool
sections.body:
When you face a real‑world problem, the first question is **what you want to find out**.  
Is it how something changes at a single instant, or is it the total amount that has accumulated over a period?  
The answer tells you whether a *derivative* or an *integral* (or sometimes both) is the right tool.

> **Definition:** A **derivative** measures the instantaneous rate of change of a quantity.  
> It answers “how fast?” at a particular moment.

> **Definition:** An **integral** adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to give a total.  
> It answers “how much in total?” over an interval.

Below are three brief scenarios. For each we identify the question, choose the appropriate calculus concept, and see why it fits.

---

### 1. Physics – Speed of a falling ball  

A ball is dropped from a height. A sensor records its position $s(t)$ (in meters) at time $t$ (in seconds).  
**Question:** What is the ball’s speed exactly 2 seconds after release?

Speed is the rate at which position changes, so we need the derivative of $s(t)$:

$$v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$$  

Evaluating $v(2)$ gives the instantaneous speed at $t=2\,$s.  
If the position function were $s(t)=5t^{2}$, then

$$v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(5t^{2})=10t,$$

and $v(2)=20\,$m/s.  

> **In daily life:** Think of a car’s speedometer. It shows the derivative of the car’s distance‑travelled curve at that exact moment.

---

### 2. Biology – Total nutrient absorbed  

A plant absorbs nutrients from soil at a rate that depends on time: $r(t)$ grams per hour. The rate varies because sunlight and temperature change throughout the day.  
**Question:** How many grams of nutrient does the plant absorb between 8 am and 2 pm?

Here we need the total amount, so we integrate the rate over the time interval:

$$\text{Total}=\int_{8}^{14} r(t)\,dt.$$  

If the rate were $r(t)=3+0.5t$ (with $t$ measured in hours after 8 am), then

$$\int_{8}^{14} (3+0.5t)\,dt
= \Big[3t+0.25t^{2}\Big]_{8}^{14}
= (42+49)-(24+16)=51\text{ grams}.$$

> **Note:** Integration is like adding up the area under the curve of $r(t)$. Each tiny rectangle represents a small amount of nutrient absorbed in a short time slice.

---

### 3. Economics – Marginal profit and total profit  

A company sells widgets. Its profit function $P(q)$ (in dollars) depends on the number $q$ of widgets produced and sold. The **marginal profit** is the derivative $P'(q)$, the extra profit from selling one more widget.  
**Question A:** What is the extra profit from the 101st widget?  
**Question B:** What is the total profit from producing the first 200 widgets if the profit at zero production is zero?

For Question A we use the derivative:

$$\text{Marginal profit at }q=100 = P'(100).$$  

If $P(q)=5q-0.01q^{2}$, then $P'(q)=5-0.02q$, so $P'(100)=5-2=3$ dollars.

For Question B we need the integral of the marginal profit, which recovers the original profit function (up to a constant). Because $P(0)=0$, the constant is zero:

$$P(200)=\int_{0}^{200} P'(q)\,dq.$$

Carrying out the integral gives the same $P(200)$ as plugging directly into $P(q)$.

> **Remember:** In economics, the derivative gives *marginal* quantities (change per extra unit), while the integral gives the *total* accumulated quantity.

---

### Putting it together  

- Use a **derivative** when the problem asks for a rate, slope, or instantaneous change.  
- Use an **integral** when the problem asks for a total amount, accumulated quantity, or area under a curve.  
- Some problems require both: first differentiate to find a rate, then integrate that rate to recover the total.

By matching the question’s wording to these ideas, you can quickly decide which calculus tool will give the answer you need.

sections.heading: 5. Worked Example: Motion Problem
sections.body:
Imagine a car moving along a straight road. At any moment we might want to know **how fast** it is going (its instantaneous velocity), **how quickly that speed is changing** (its acceleration), and **how far** it has travelled over a time interval.  
All three quantities can be obtained from the same piece of information: the position of the car as a function of time, say  

$$s(t)=5t^{2}+2t+1,$$  

where $s$ is measured in meters and $t$ in seconds.

> **Definition:** *Instantaneous velocity* is the limit of the average velocity over a shrinking time interval. It tells us the exact speed at a single instant.

### Step 1 – Find the instantaneous velocity using a limit  

The average velocity between times $t$ and $t+\Delta t$ is  

$$\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

To get the instantaneous velocity at time $t$, we let the interval $\Delta t$ become *infinitely small* and take a limit:

$$v(t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

Plug the given $s(t)$ into the fraction:

\[
\frac{(5(t+\Delta t)^{2}+2(t+\Delta t)+1)-(5t^{2}+2t+1)}{\Delta t}
\]

Expand the numerator:

\[
\frac{5(t^{2}+2t\Delta t+(\Delta t)^{2})+2t+2\Delta t+1-5t^{2}-2t-1}{\Delta t}
= \frac{10t\Delta t+5(\Delta t)^{2}+2\Delta t}{\Delta t}.
\]

Cancel $\Delta t$:

\[
10t+5\Delta t+2.
\]

Now let $\Delta t\to 0$:

$$v(t)=10t+2.$$

So at any moment $t$, the car’s velocity is $10t+2$ meters per second.

> **In daily life:** This is like checking a speedometer that updates continuously; the limit process is the math behind that smooth reading.

### Step 2 – Differentiate to obtain acceleration  

Acceleration tells us how fast the velocity itself is changing. It is the derivative of $v(t)$ with respect to $t$:

$$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}.$$

Since $v(t)=10t+2$, differentiate term by term:

$$a(t)=10.$$

The acceleration is constant: the car speeds up by $10\ \text{m/s}^2$ at every instant.

> **Note:** Differentiation is the formal name for the limit process we used earlier. Once we have a formula for velocity, taking its derivative gives acceleration directly.

### Step 3 – Integrate to find the distance travelled  

Suppose we want the total distance the car travels from $t=0$ to $t=3$ seconds. Integration is the reverse of differentiation: it adds up infinitely many tiny pieces of motion. The distance $D$ is

$$D=\int_{0}^{3} v(t)\,dt.$$

Insert $v(t)=10t+2$:

$$D=\int_{0}^{3} (10t+2)\,dt.$$

Integrate term by term:

\[
\int (10t)\,dt =5t^{2},\qquad \int 2\,dt =2t.
\]

Thus  

$$D=\Bigl[5t^{2}+2t\Bigr]_{0}^{3}= \bigl(5\cdot 3^{2}+2\cdot 3\bigr)-\bigl(5\cdot0^{2}+2\cdot0\bigr)=45+6=51\ \text{meters}.$$

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to evaluate the antiderivative at both limits. Always subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit.

### Putting it all together  

1. **Limit** → instantaneous velocity $v(t)=10t+2$.  
2. **Derivative** (differentiating $v$) → constant acceleration $a(t)=10$.  
3. **Integral** (adding up $v$ over time) → total distance $51\,$m from $0$ to $3\,$s.

> **Remember:** Limits, derivatives, and integrals are three faces of the same idea—how quantities change and accumulate. Mastering each step lets you move smoothly from position → velocity → acceleration, and back from velocity → distance.

sections.heading: 6. Worked Example: Population Growth
sections.body:
Imagine a town where the number of people does not grow forever. At first, when there are few residents, each family can have many children, so the population rises quickly. As the town becomes crowded, there is less space, food, and jobs, so the growth slows down and eventually levels off.  
This idea is captured by the **logistic model**, a simple formula that describes how a population changes over time while respecting a maximum size, called the *carrying capacity*.

> **Definition:** The *carrying capacity* $K$ is the largest population that the environment can sustain indefinitely.

---

### 1. From a limit to the growth rate  

The *instantaneous growth rate* tells us how fast the population is changing at a particular moment. Mathematically, it is the limit of the average change over a very short time interval.

If $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$, the average change from $t$ to $t+\Delta t$ is  

$$\frac{P(t+\Delta t)-P(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

Taking the limit as $\Delta t\to 0$ gives the **derivative**:

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{P(t+\Delta t)-P(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

This derivative is the instantaneous growth rate, measured in people per unit time.

> **Note:** A derivative is just a precise way of saying “how fast something is changing right now”.

---

### 2. Writing the logistic differential equation  

The logistic model assumes two things:

1. When the population is small, it grows proportionally to its current size. This gives a term $rP$, where $r$ is the *intrinsic growth rate* (how fast the population would grow without limits).
2. As the population approaches $K$, the growth slows down. The slowdown is proportional to both the current size $P$ and the fraction of unused capacity $\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$.

Combining these ideas, the *logistic differential equation* is  

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).$$

Here $r>0$ and $K>0$ are constants that depend on the species and environment.

> **In daily life:** Think of a bathtub filling with water. The faucet supplies water at a constant rate, but as the tub fills, the water level rises more slowly because the space left is smaller. The logistic equation works the same way for populations.

---

### 3. Solving the differential equation (finding $P(t)$)

To predict the future population, we need to *integrate* the equation. First, separate the variables $P$ and $t$:

$$\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)}\,dP = r\,dt.$$

The left side can be split using partial fractions:

$$\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)}=\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}.$$

Now integrate both sides:

$$\int\left(\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}\right)dP = \int r\,dt.$$

Carrying out the integrals gives

$$\ln|P| - \ln|K-P| = rt + C,$$

where $C$ is the constant of integration, determined by the initial population $P(0)=P_0$.

Combine the logarithms:

$$\ln\left(\frac{P}{K-P}\right)=rt + C.$$

Exponentiate to remove the log:

$$\frac{P}{K-P}=Ae^{rt},\qquad A=e^{C}.$$

Solve for $P$:

$$P(t)=\frac{K\,Ae^{rt}}{1+Ae^{rt}}.$$

Use the initial condition $P(0)=P_0$ to find $A$:

$$\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}=A,$$

so $A=\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}$. Substituting back,

$$\boxed{\,P(t)=\frac{K}{1+\left(\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}\,}.$$

This formula predicts the population at any future time $t$.

> **Remember:** The logistic curve starts near exponential growth, then bends and approaches the horizontal line $P=K$ as $t\to\infty$.

---

### 4. Using the model: a concrete example  

Suppose a wildlife reserve can support at most $K=10{,}000$ deer. The intrinsic growth rate is $r=0.4$ per year, and the current population is $P_0=1{,}000$ deer.

First compute the factor $\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}= \frac{9{,}000}{1{,}000}=9$.

The population after $t$ years is

$$P(t)=\frac{10{,}000}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}.$$

If we want the population after 5 years, plug in $t=5$:

$$P(5)=\frac{10{,}000}{1+9e^{-2}} \approx \frac{10{,}000}{1+9(0.135)} \approx \frac{10{,}000}{2.215} \approx 4{,}514\text{ deer}.$$

The model shows rapid growth at first, then a slowdown as the reserve fills.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include the factor $\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$ leads to the simple exponential model, which predicts unlimited growth—unrealistic for most real‑world populations.

---

By defining the growth rate with a limit, turning the logistic idea into a differential equation, and then integrating, we obtain a powerful tool for forecasting how populations evolve over time. This step‑by‑step process mirrors many problems in calculus: start with a real‑world description, translate it into mathematics, and use limits, derivatives, and integrals to find answers.

sections.heading: 7. Reflection and Practice
sections.body:
Reflection and practice are the best ways to turn new ideas into lasting skills.  
In this part you will see how a problem can be broken into three clear stages:

1. **Limit** – find the instantaneous rate or the behaviour at a point.  
2. **Derivative** – turn that limit into a formula that works for any $x$.  
3. **Integral** – use the derivative (or its inverse) to accumulate change over an interval.

When you can recognise which stage you are in, you can choose the right tool – just like picking the right screwdriver for a screw.

> **Remember:** The three steps are a *sequence*: limit → derivative → integral.  
> If you skip a step, you may end up with an answer that looks right but is actually based on a hidden assumption.

Below is a mixed problem set. For each question, follow the guide:

* **Step 1 – Identify the limit.** Write down the limit expression that describes the situation.  
* **Step 2 – Compute the derivative.** Turn the limit into a derivative function $f'(x)$.  
* **Step 3 – Set up the integral.** Decide what quantity you need to add up (area, total change, etc.) and write the appropriate integral.  
* **Step 4 – Check.** Plug the result back into the original story to see if it makes sense.

---

### Problem 1: Speed of a car

A car’s position along a straight road is given by $s(t)=3t^{2}+2t$ meters, where $t$ is time in seconds.

1. **Limit:** Write the limit that defines the car’s instantaneous speed at time $t=4$ seconds.  
2. **Derivative:** Compute $s'(t)$, the speed function.  
3. **Integral:** Find the total distance traveled from $t=2$ s to $t=5$ s by integrating the speed.  

*Hint:* The distance is $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} s'(t)\,dt$.

---

### Problem 2: Water flowing into a tank

Water flows into a cylindrical tank at a rate that changes with time: the flow rate (in liters per minute) is $r(t)=5\sin(t)+10$, where $t$ is minutes after the tap is opened.

1. **Limit:** Express the instantaneous flow rate at $t=\pi$ minutes as a limit.  
2. **Derivative:** The flow rate itself is already a function of $t$, so $r'(t)$ would represent how the flow rate is changing. Compute $r'(t)$.  
3. **Integral:** How many liters are in the tank after 4 minutes? Use an integral of $r(t)$ from $0$ to $4$.  

*Check:* The answer should be a positive number; if you obtain a negative, you have likely reversed the limits.

---

### Problem 3: Bacterial population

A bacterial culture grows according to $P(t)=P_{0}e^{0.3t}$, where $P_{0}=200$ cells and $t$ is measured in hours.

1. **Limit:** Write the limit that gives the instantaneous growth rate at $t=3$ h.  
2. **Derivative:** Find $P'(t)$, the rate at which the number of cells changes.  
3. **Integral:** Suppose you want the total increase in cell count from $t=0$ to $t=5$ h. Set up and evaluate the integral of $P'(t)$.  

$$\int_{0}^{5} P'(t)\,dt = P(5)-P(0)$$  

*Why this works:* Integrating the derivative over an interval gives the net change of the original function.

---

### Problem 4: Temperature change

The temperature in a room (in °C) varies with time according to $T(t)=20+4\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{12}\right)$, where $t$ is hours after midnight.

1. **Limit:** Write the limit that would give the instantaneous rate of temperature change at $t=6$ h.  
2. **Derivative:** Compute $T'(t)$.  
3. **Integral:** How much does the temperature increase or decrease between $t=0$ and $t=12$? Use the integral of $T'(t)$.  

*Interpretation:* A positive integral means overall warming; a negative integral means overall cooling.

---

### How to check your work

- **Units:** Make sure the units match at each step (e.g., meters per second for speed, liters for volume).  
- **Reasonableness:** Ask yourself if the number seems plausible. A car traveling at $1000\,$m/s is unrealistic, so you probably made an algebra slip.  
- **Reverse step:** After integrating, differentiate your answer. You should get back the original derivative function (up to a constant).  

> **In daily life:** Think of the three steps like a recipe. The limit is tasting a single bite to know the flavor, the derivative is writing down the full recipe, and the integral is cooking the whole meal and measuring how much you end up with.

Work through each problem slowly, writing out every limit, derivative, and integral. When you finish, compare your answers with a classmate or the answer key. The more you practice spotting the sequence, the quicker you’ll know which tool to reach for next time.

examples.title: Linear Motion – Finding Velocity
examples.given: A car travels along a straight road with position $s(t)=5t^{2}+2t$ (meters) at time $t$ seconds. Find the instantaneous velocity at $t=3\ \text{s}$.

steps.label: Differentiate Position
steps.text: Compute $v(t)=\dfrac{ds}{dt}=10t+2$ using the power rule, because velocity is the derivative of position.

examples.answer: The car’s instantaneous velocity at $3\ \text{s}$ is $32\ \text{m/s}$. ---

examples.title: Population Growth – Choosing a Model
examples.given: A town’s population $P(t)$ (in thousands) follows $P(t)=P_{0}e^{kt}$, where $t$ is years after 2020. In 2020, $P_{0}=50$. After 5 years, the population is $65$ thousand. Determine the growth rate $k$ and predict the population in 2030.

steps.label: Solve for $k$
steps.text: Divide by 50: $e^{5k}=1.3$. Take natural log: $5k=\ln 1.3$, so $k=\dfrac{\ln 1.3}{5}$.

examples.answer: The growth rate is $k\approx0.0525\ \text{yr}^{-1}$ and the predicted 2030 population is about $84.5$ thousand people. ---

examples.title: Optimizing Cost – Choosing the Right Tool
examples.given: A company can produce a widget either by manual labor (cost $C_m(x)=20x+500$ dollars for $x$ units) or by an automated machine (cost $C_a(x)=15x+1200$ dollars). Determine for which production levels $x$ the manual method is cheaper, and find the break‑even point where both costs are equal.

steps.label: Set costs equal
steps.text: Solve $20x+500=15x+1200$ to find the break‑even quantity.

steps.label: Isolate $x$
steps.text: Subtract $15x$ from both sides: $5x+500=1200$. Then subtract 500: $5x=700$.

examples.answer: The manual method is cheaper when producing fewer than $140$ widgets; the automated machine is cheaper when producing more than $140$ widgets. The break‑even point is at $x=140$ units.

practice.q: Find the derivative of $f(x)=3x^2+5x-2$.
practice.a:
The derivative of a polynomial is found by applying the power rule $ \frac{d}{dx}[x^n]=nx^{n-1} $.
- For $3x^2$: $ \frac{d}{dx}[3x^2]=3\cdot2x^{2-1}=6x$.
- For $5x$: $ \frac{d}{dx}[5x]=5\cdot1x^{1-1}=5$.
- For the constant $-2$: $ \frac{d}{dx}[-2]=0$.
Combine the terms: $f'(x)=6x+5$.

practice.q: Compute $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}$.
practice.a:
Factor the numerator: $x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)$.
Then $\displaystyle \frac{x^2-9}{x-3}=\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=x+3$, for $x\neq3$.
Now take the limit: $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to3}(x+3)=3+3=6$.

practice.q: A particle moves along a line with position $s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t$ (meters) for $t\ge0$. Find its velocity at $t=2$ seconds and the total distance traveled from $t=0$ to $t=3$ seconds.
practice.a:
Velocity is the derivative of position: $v(t)=s'(t)=3t^2-12t+9$.
- At $t=2$: $v(2)=3(2)^2-12(2)+9=12-24+9=-3\,$m/s.
To find total distance, locate where velocity changes sign: solve $v(t)=0$.
$3t^2-12t+9=0 \;\Rightarrow\; t^2-4t+3=0 \;\Rightarrow\; (t-1)(t-3)=0$, so $t=1$ and $t=3$.
Check intervals:
- $0\le t<1$: pick $t=0.5$, $v(0.5)=3(0.25)-12(0.5)+9=0.75-6+9=3.75>0$.
- $1<t<3$: pick $t=2$, $v(2)=-3<0$.
- $t>3$: $v$ becomes positive again.
Distance = $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}v(t)\,dt -\int_{1}^{3}v(t)\,dt$ (subtract because velocity is negative on $[1,3]$).
Compute antiderivative $S(t)=\int v(t)dt = t^3-6t^2+9t$ (which is just $s(t)$).
- $\int_{0}^{1}v(t)dt = s(1)-s(0)= (1-6+9)-(0)=4$.
- $\int_{1}^{3}v(t)dt = s(3)-s(1)= (27-54+27)-4=0-4=-4$.
Take absolute value: distance $=4-(-4)=8$ meters.

practice.q: Evaluate the definite integral $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2} (4x-5)\,dx$ and interpret its meaning as the net change of the function $F(x)=2x^2-5x$ over $[0,2]$.
practice.a:
Antiderivative of $4x-5$ is $F(x)=2x^2-5x$.
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:
$\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2} (4x-5)\,dx = F(2)-F(0)$.
Compute: $F(2)=2(2)^2-5(2)=8-10=-2$, $F(0)=0$.
Thus the integral equals $-2-0=-2$.
Interpretation: The net change of $F$ from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is $-2$; $F$ decreased by 2 units over that interval.

practice.q: The population $P(t)$ of a bacteria culture satisfies the differential equation $\displaystyle \frac{dP}{dt}=0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{5000}\right)$ with $P(0)=1000$. Find an explicit formula for $P(t)$ and determine the population after 10 hours.
practice.a:
This is a logistic differential equation: $\displaystyle \frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{M}\right)$ with $k=0.4$, $M=5000$.
Separate variables:
$\displaystyle \frac{dP}{P(1-P/5000)} = 0.4\,dt$.
Partial fractions: $\displaystyle \frac{1}{P(1-P/5000)} = \frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\,\frac{1}{5000}$.
Carrying out the decomposition gives:
$\displaystyle \frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\frac{1}{5000} = \frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\frac{1}{5000}$ (standard result).
Integrate:
$\displaystyle \int\left(\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{5000-P}\frac{1}{5000}\right)dP = 0.4\int dt$.
Simplify: $\displaystyle \ln|P| - \ln|5000-P| = 0.4t + C$.
Combine logs: $\displaystyle \ln\left|\frac{P}{5000-P}\right| = 0.4t + C$.
Exponentiate: $\displaystyle \frac{P}{5000-P}=Ce^{0.4t}$.
Solve for $P$: $P = 5000\frac{Ce^{0.4t}}{1+Ce^{0.4t}}$.
Use initial condition $P(0)=1000$:
$\displaystyle \frac{1000}{5000-1000}= \frac{1000}{4000}= \frac14 = C e^{0}=C$.
Thus $C= \frac14$.
Plug back:
$P(t)=5000\frac{(1/4)e^{0.4t}}{1+(1/4)e^{0.4t}} = \frac{5000 e^{0.4t}}{4+ e^{0.4t}}$.
Now compute $P(10)$:
$e^{0.4\cdot10}=e^{4}\approx 54.598$.
$P(10)=\frac{5000\cdot54.598}{4+54.598}= \frac{272990}{58.598}\approx 4662\text{ (rounded)}$.
So after 10 hours the population is about $4.66\times10^{3}$ bacteria.

practice.q: Find the limit $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin(5x)-5x}{x^3}$.
practice.a:
Use the Taylor series for $\sin(5x)$ around $0$:
$\sin(5x)=5x-\frac{(5x)^3}{3!}+ \frac{(5x)^5}{5!}-\dots =5x-\frac{125x^3}{6}+O(x^5)$.
Subtract $5x$: $\sin(5x)-5x = -\frac{125x^3}{6}+O(x^5)$.
Divide by $x^3$: $\displaystyle \frac{\sin(5x)-5x}{x^3}= -\frac{125}{6}+O(x^2)$.
Taking the limit as $x\to0$, the $O(x^2)$ term vanishes, leaving
$\displaystyle \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(5x)-5x}{x^3}= -\frac{125}{6}$.

data.recap: The lesson explained limits as the value a function approaches, showed how derivatives are limits of difference quotients that give instantaneous rates of change, introduced integrals as the inverse of derivatives via the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and gave guidance on choosing between derivatives and integrals for real‑world problems.

key_terms.meaning: The value a function gets arbitrarily close to as the input approaches a certain point.
The instantaneous rate of change of a function, defined as the limit of the difference quotient.
The average rate of change (f(a+h)-f(a))/h used to define the derivative.
The accumulation of infinitely many tiny pieces, giving the total change of a function over an interval.
States that the integral of a continuous function from a to b equals an antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints, linking derivatives and integrals.
The limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero.
The maximum population size that an environment can sustain indefinitely.
A function whose derivative is the given function.

quiz.q: What does the limit lim x->a f(x)=L mean?
options: f(x) equals L for all x
f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a
L is the maximum value of f(x)
quiz.why: A limit describes the behavior of the function near a point, not necessarily at the point.

quiz.q: Which expression defines the derivative of f at x=a?
options: integral from a to a+ h of f(x) dx
quiz.why: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient as the step h approaches zero.

quiz.q: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus connects which two concepts?
quiz.why: It shows that integration and differentiation are inverse operations.

quiz.q: If s(t)=5t^2+2t+1, what is the instantaneous velocity at time t?
quiz.why: Differentiating s(t) gives v(t)=ds/dt=10t+2, the instantaneous velocity.

quiz.q: In a logistic growth model, what does the symbol K represent?
quiz.why: K denotes the maximum sustainable population size.

quiz.q: Which tool would you use to find the total distance traveled from t=0 to t=3 given a velocity function v(t)?
options: Average of v(t) at t=0 and t=3
quiz.why: Integrating velocity over an interval gives total distance traveled.

Instantaneous rate of change; limit of the difference quotient.
(f(a+h)-f(a))/h, the average rate of change over a small interval.
Sum of infinitely many tiny pieces; gives total accumulation over an interval.
Integral of f from a to b equals antiderivative F evaluated at b minus F at a.

data.summary: Lesson 12 applies limits, derivatives, and integrals to real‑world problems in physics, biology, and economics. Students practice setting up and solving calculus models to build confidence in using these tools.
objectives: Translate a word problem into a limit, derivative, or integral expression
Compute the required calculus quantity using appropriate rules
Interpret the mathematical result in the context of the original problem
Explain how changing assumptions affects the model outcome
Present a clear, step‑by‑step solution to a real‑world scenario
data.prerequisites: Students should already know limits, continuity, derivative rules, basic integration techniques, and how to evaluate definite integrals.
why: Calculus is the language of change and accumulation. In physics it predicts motion, in biology it describes population growth, and in economics it measures cost, revenue, and profit over time. Understanding how to build and solve these models lets students analyze real phenomena rather than just manipulate symbols.

Being able to apply calculus to authentic problems prepares students for college STEM courses and many careers. It also develops logical thinking, problem‑solving confidence, and the ability to communicate quantitative ideas clearly.

sections.heading: 1. From Word Problem to Mathematical Model
sections.body:
When we first see a word problem, the goal is to turn the story into a clean mathematical picture.  
Think of it like translating a foreign language: we need to pick the right “words” (variables) and the right “grammar” (operations) so the problem can be solved with calculus.

> **Definition:** *Variable* – a symbol that stands for a quantity that can change.  
> **Note:** Choose a variable that captures the most important changing quantity in the problem.

**Step 1 – Identify the variable**  
Read the problem carefully and ask: *What is changing, and what do we want to know about that change?*  
For example, in a story about a tank being filled with water, the amount of water in the tank grows over time. We would let  

$$
V(t) = \text{volume of water in the tank at time } t
$$  

Here the variable is \(V\) and the independent variable (the thing we measure against) is time \(t\).

**Step 2 – Decide the type of relationship**  
Ask yourself whether the problem talks about a *rate of change* (how fast something is changing) or an *accumulation* (how much has built up).  

- **Rate of change** means we are interested in the instantaneous speed of the variable. In calculus this is expressed by a *derivative*.  
- **Accumulation** means we want the total amount gathered over an interval. In calculus this is expressed by an *integral*.

> **In daily life:** When you watch a car’s speedometer, you see the rate of change of distance with respect to time. When you look at the odometer, you see the accumulated distance.

**Step 3 – Write the appropriate limit expression**  
Both derivatives and integrals are defined using limits, which capture the idea of “getting arbitrarily close” to a value.

- If the problem involves a rate, write the derivative as a limit:

$$
\frac{dV}{dt} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{V(t+\Delta t)-V(t)}{\Delta t}
$$

This says: “the instantaneous change of \(V\) at time \(t\) is the limit of the average change over a tiny time interval \(\Delta t\) as that interval shrinks to zero.”

- If the problem involves accumulation, write the integral as a limit of sums (a *Riemann sum*):

$$
\int_{a}^{b} f(t)\,dt = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(t_i^*)\Delta t_i
$$

Here \(f(t)\) is the rate at which something is added, \(\Delta t_i\) are small time pieces, and the sum adds up all those tiny contributions. The limit makes the pieces infinitesimally small, giving the exact total.

**Step 4 – Connect the expression to the story**  
Replace the generic symbols with the ones from the problem.  
If the story says “water flows in at 3 L/min,” then the rate function is \(f(t)=3\) (constant). The accumulated volume from time \(a\) to \(b\) becomes

$$
V(b)-V(a)=\int_{a}^{b} 3\,dt = 3(b-a).
$$

If the story instead says “the water level rises faster as the tank gets fuller,” we might have a rate like \(f(t)=kV(t)\). Then the derivative form

$$
\frac{dV}{dt}=kV(t)
$$

captures the exponential growth described in the word problem.

> **Remember:** The choice between derivative and integral is guided by the question: *Are we looking for how fast something changes (derivative) or how much has been added over time (integral)?*

**Step 5 – Check the units**  
Make sure the units on both sides of your equation match. In the derivative example, \(\frac{dV}{dt}\) has units of volume per time (e.g., liters per minute). In the integral example, the result has units of volume, because we multiply a rate (volume per time) by a time interval.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include the differential \(dt\) in an integral. Writing \(\int_{a}^{b} f(t)\) without “\(dt\)” loses the connection to the variable of integration and makes the expression dimensionally incorrect.

By following these small, clear steps—pick a variable, decide if you need a rate or an accumulation, write the limit‑based derivative or integral, and then translate back to the story—you turn any word problem into a mathematical model ready for calculus tools. This systematic translation is the foundation for solving the later examples in physics, biology, and economics.

sections.heading: 2. Physics Example: Falling Object
sections.body:
Imagine you drop a ball from the top of a building. You can watch it fall, but how do we describe its motion with numbers?  In physics we use **position** $s(t)$ (how far the ball is from the ground at time $t$), **velocity** $v(t)$ (how fast the position is changing), and **acceleration** $a(t)$ (how fast the velocity is changing).  These three ideas are linked by calculus:  

> **Definition:** The *derivative* of a function gives its instantaneous rate of change.  
> **Definition:** The *integral* of a function adds up tiny pieces to give a total amount.

---

### Step 1 – Write down the acceleration

Near the Earth’s surface the only important force on a falling object is gravity.  Gravity gives a constant downward acceleration  

\[
a(t)= -g,
\]

where $g\approx 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ and the minus sign shows the direction is toward the ground.  The unit “meters per second squared” (m/s²) tells us how many meters per second the velocity changes each second.

---

### Step 2 – Find the velocity by integrating acceleration

Integration is the reverse of differentiation.  To get velocity we add up all the tiny changes in speed that occur over time:

\[
v(t)=\int a(t)\,dt = \int (-g)\,dt = -g t + C_1 .
\]

The symbol $C_1$ is a **constant of integration**.  It represents the velocity the ball had at the moment we started counting time.  If we release the ball from rest, then at $t=0$ the velocity is $0$, so

\[
0 = -g\cdot 0 + C_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_1 = 0 .
\]

Thus the velocity formula simplifies to  

\[
v(t)= -g t .
\]

The unit of $v(t)$ is meters per second (m/s).  The negative sign again tells us the ball is moving downward.

> **In daily life:** When you throw a ball straight up, its velocity is positive while it rises and becomes negative after it starts falling—exactly what the sign in $v(t)$ indicates.

---

### Step 3 – Find the position by integrating velocity

Now we add up all the tiny distances the ball travels as its speed changes:

\[
s(t)=\int v(t)\,dt = \int (-g t)\,dt = -\frac{1}{2}g t^{2}+ C_2 .
\]

$C_2$ is another constant of integration.  It tells us where the ball started.  Suppose the ball is dropped from a height $h$ above the ground.  At $t=0$, the position is $s(0)=h$, so

\[
h = -\frac{1}{2}g\cdot 0^{2}+ C_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_2 = h .
\]

Therefore the position as a function of time is  

\[
s(t)= h - \frac{1}{2}g t^{2}.
\]

The unit of $s(t)$ is meters (m).  As time grows, the term $\frac{1}{2}g t^{2}$ becomes larger, so $s(t)$ gets smaller—meaning the ball gets closer to the ground.

> **Note:** The formula $s(t)=h-\frac12gt^{2}$ works only while the ball is falling freely.  If it hits the ground, the model must change.

---

### Step 4 – Check the result with a simple question

How long does it take the ball to hit the ground?  Set $s(t)=0$ (ground level) and solve for $t$:

\[
0 = h - \frac{1}{2}g t^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{1}{2}g t^{2}=h
\;\Longrightarrow\;
t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} .
\]

If $h=20\ \text{m}$, then  

\[
t = \sqrt{\frac{2\cdot20}{9.8}} \approx 2.02\ \text{s}.
\]

Plugging $t=2.02\ \text{s}$ back into $v(t) = -g t$ gives  

\[
v(2.02) \approx -9.8 \times 2.02 \approx -19.8\ \text{m/s},
\]

a speed that makes sense for a falling object after about two seconds.

> **Remember:** Always keep track of units.  If you accidentally mix seconds with minutes, the numbers will be wrong even though the algebra looks correct.

---

### Step 5 – Summarize the chain of ideas

1. **Acceleration** is given (constant $-g$).  
2. **Integrate** acceleration → velocity, adding a constant that matches the initial speed.  
3. **Integrate** velocity → position, adding a constant that matches the starting height.  
4. **Use** the position formula to answer practical questions (time to hit ground, speed at impact).

By moving from the physical description (a ball falling) to the mathematical model (derivatives and integrals), we can predict exactly how fast and how far the ball moves at any moment. This same process—turning a word problem into equations, then solving step by step—will appear throughout calculus and many other sciences.

sections.heading: 3. Biology Example: Logistic Population Growth
sections.body:
Imagine a small island where a certain type of rabbit lives. At first there are only a few rabbits, so they have plenty of food and space. As the population grows, food becomes scarcer and the island can only hold so many rabbits before crowding stops further growth. This idea – that a population grows quickly when it is small but slows down as it approaches a limit – is captured by the **logistic model**.

> **Definition:** *Carrying capacity* ($K$) is the maximum number of individuals that an environment can sustain indefinitely.

### 1. From a word problem to a differential equation  

We want a formula that tells us how the rabbit population $P(t)$ changes over time $t$. Two forces act on the population:

1. **Natural growth** – when there is plenty of food, the population tends to increase proportionally to its current size. This gives the term $rP$, where $r>0$ is the *intrinsic growth rate* (how fast the rabbits would grow without limits).

2. **Limiting effect** – as the population approaches the carrying capacity $K$, the growth slows down. A simple way to model this slowdown is to multiply the natural growth term by a factor that becomes smaller as $P$ gets close to $K$. The factor $\displaystyle 1-\frac{P}{K}$ does exactly that: it is near $1$ when $P\ll K$ and goes to $0$ when $P=K$.

Putting these ideas together gives the **logistic differential equation**  

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).
$$

> **Note:** A *differential equation* relates a function (here $P(t)$) to its derivative (its rate of change). Solving it means finding the function itself.

### 2. Solving by separation of variables  

“Separation of variables’’ means we rearrange the equation so that all terms involving $P$ are on one side and all terms involving $t$ are on the other.

Start with  

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).
$$

Divide both sides by $P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$ and multiply by $dt$:

$$
\frac{dP}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)} = r\,dt.
$$

Now we need to integrate both sides. The left side looks messy, but we can split it using *partial fractions*:

\[
\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)}=
\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}\;\frac{1}{K}.
\]

More explicitly,

\[
\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)}=
\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}\;\frac{1}{K}.
\]

Integrating gives  

$$
\int\!\left(\frac{1}{P}+\frac{1}{K-P}\right)dP = \int r\,dt .
$$

The integrals are straightforward:

\[
\ln|P| - \ln|K-P| = rt + C,
\]

where $C$ is the constant of integration. Combine the logarithms:

\[
\ln\!\left(\frac{P}{K-P}\right)=rt + C.
\]

Exponentiate both sides to remove the log:

\[
\frac{P}{K-P}=Ce^{rt},
\]

with $C=e^{C}$ (still a constant). Solve for $P$:

\[
P = \frac{KCe^{rt}}{1+Ce^{rt}}.
\]

To determine $C$, use the initial population $P(0)=P_0$:

\[
\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}=C.
\]

Substituting back, the final **logistic solution** is  

$$
P(t)=\frac{K}{1+\left(\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}.
$$

> **In daily life:** This formula tells you how a virus spreads in a closed community, how a fishery recovers after over‑fishing, or how a startup’s user base grows before hitting market saturation.

### 3. Interpreting the result  

- When $t\to\infty$, the exponential term $e^{-rt}\to0$, so  

\[
P(t)\to\frac{K}{1+0}=K.
\]

  The population settles at the **carrying capacity** $K$. No matter how many rabbits you start with (as long as $P_0>0$), the island cannot support more than $K$ rabbits in the long run.

- If $P_0$ is very small, the denominator is initially close to $1$, and $P(t)$ grows almost like $P(t)\approx P_0e^{rt}$, the familiar exponential growth. This matches our intuition: when there is plenty of room, the rabbits multiply quickly.

- If $P_0$ is already near $K$, the fraction $\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}$ is small, so the denominator is already larger than $1$, and growth is slow from the start.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include the factor $\displaystyle 1-\frac{P}{K}$ leads to the simple exponential model $\frac{dP}{dt}=rP$, which predicts unlimited growth – unrealistic for most real‑world populations.

### 4. Why this matters  

Understanding the logistic model helps biologists predict how species will respond to changes in habitat, how conservation efforts might raise $K$, or how disease control measures affect the effective carrying capacity of a pathogen. The math shows that **limits matter**: growth cannot continue forever, and the shape of the curve tells us *when* the limit will start to dominate.

> **Remember:** The logistic equation balances *growth* ($rP$) with *restriction* ($1-P/K$). Solving it gives a smooth S‑shaped curve that starts fast, slows down, and finally levels off at the carrying capacity $K$.

sections.heading: 4. Economics Example: Consumer Surplus
sections.body:
Imagine you go to a market and see a table of prices for a product—say, a concert ticket. The price you actually pay is the **market price**. But each buyer might have been willing to pay a different amount, depending on how much they value the experience. The **consumer surplus** is the total amount of “extra happiness” that all buyers get because they pay less than what they were prepared to pay.

> **Definition:** *Consumer surplus* is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a good and what they actually pay.

---

### 1.  Modelling demand as a function  

Economists often describe how much of a product people want at each price with a **demand function**.  
Let $p$ denote the price (in dollars) and $q(p)$ the quantity demanded at that price.  
A simple linear demand curve looks like  

$$
q(p)=a-bp,
$$  

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.  
- $a$ is the quantity demanded if the price were $0$ (the “maximum possible demand”).  
- $b$ tells us how quickly demand falls as price rises.

**Example:** Suppose a small bakery sells cupcakes. If the price were free, 200 people would take one ($a=200$). For each extra dollar, 10 fewer people buy a cupcake, so $b=10$. The demand function is  

$$
q(p)=200-10p.
$$

---

### 2.  From demand to willingness to pay  

The **willingness to pay** for each individual unit is represented by the area under the demand curve from the price you actually pay, $p_0$, up to the highest price anyone would pay (where $q=0$).  
First find that highest price $p_{\max}$ by setting $q(p)=0$:

$$
0 = a - b p_{\max} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_{\max}= \frac{a}{b}.
$$

In the cupcake example, $p_{\max}=200/10 = 20$ dollars. No one would buy a cupcake if it cost more than \$20.

The total willingness to pay for all cupcakes sold at price $p_0$ is the **definite integral** of the demand function from $p_0$ to $p_{\max}$:

$$
\text{WTP}= \int_{p_0}^{p_{\max}} q(p)\,dp.
$$

Plugging the linear form gives  

$$
\text{WTP}= \int_{p_0}^{p_{\max}} (a-bp)\,dp
          = \Big[ap-\tfrac{b}{2}p^{2}\Big]_{p_0}^{p_{\max}}.
$$

---

### 3.  Subtract actual expenditure  

The **actual expenditure** is simply the market price times the quantity actually bought:

$$
\text{Expenditure}= p_0 \, q(p_0).
$$

Finally, the consumer surplus $CS$ is  

$$
CS = \text{WTP} - \text{Expenditure}.
$$

---

### 4.  Worked example  

Take the cupcake shop again. Suppose the market price is $p_0 = 5$ dollars.

1. **Quantity sold**: $q(5)=200-10\cdot5 = 150$ cupcakes.  
2. **WTP**:  

\[
\text{WTP}= \Big[200p-\tfrac{10}{2}p^{2}\Big]_{5}^{20}
          = \Big[200p-5p^{2}\Big]_{5}^{20}
          = (200\cdot20-5\cdot20^{2})-(200\cdot5-5\cdot5^{2})
          = (4000-2000)-(1000-125)=2000-875=1125.
\]

3. **Expenditure**: $5 \times 150 = 750$ dollars.  

4. **Consumer surplus**:  

$$
CS = 1125 - 750 = 375 \text{ dollars}.
$$

So the 150 customers together enjoy \$375 of extra benefit because they each paid only \$5 instead of their individual higher willingness to pay.

> **In daily life:** Think of a sale where you buy a shirt for \$30, but you would have been happy to pay up to \$50. Your personal surplus is \$20. Adding up all customers’ surpluses gives the market’s consumer surplus.

---

### 5.  Why this matters  

Consumer surplus tells businesses and policymakers how much value consumers receive beyond the price tag. A large surplus suggests the product is priced well below what people value it at, which can indicate strong demand or a competitive market. Conversely, a tiny surplus may signal that prices are too high or that consumers are indifferent.

> **Remember:** The integral captures *all* the tiny willingness‑to‑pay amounts for each infinitesimal slice of quantity; adding them up gives the total benefit.

---

### 6.  Common mistake to avoid  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to integrate from the market price $p_0$ up to $p_{\max}$, and instead integrating from $0$ to $p_{\max}$. That would count willingness to pay for units that were never bought, inflating the surplus.

By carefully modelling demand, computing the integral, and subtracting the actual spending, you obtain a clear, quantitative picture of consumer surplus—an essential tool in economics.

sections.heading: 5. Checking and Interpreting Results
sections.body:
When we finish a calculation, the work is not done until we **check** that the answer makes sense.  
Checking means three things:

1. **Units** – do the numbers have the right physical units (seconds, meters, dollars …)?  
2. **Interpretation** – what does the number actually tell us about the situation?  
3. **Sensitivity** – how would the answer change if we tweaked a key parameter such as gravity, a growth rate, or a price?

Doing these steps prevents us from accepting a mathematically correct but practically useless result.

---

> **Definition:** *Units* are the labels that tell us what a number measures (e.g., meters for distance, seconds for time). Keeping track of units is a simple way to catch algebraic mistakes.

### 1. Verify the units

Suppose we modeled a falling object and found the time to hit the ground to be  

$$t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$$  

where $h$ is the height (in meters) and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity (in meters per second squared).  

Insert the units:

\[
\sqrt{\frac{2\;\text{m}}{\text{m/s}^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{m}}{\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}}}= \sqrt{\text{s}^2}= \text{s}.
\]

The result is in seconds, exactly what we expect for a time. If we had mistakenly written $g$ as $9.8$ without units, the square‑root would have given a number with no unit, signalling an error.

### 2. Interpret the numerical answer

Imagine $h = 20\,$m and $g = 9.8\,$m/s\(^2\). Plugging in:

$$t = \sqrt{\frac{2\cdot20}{9.8}} \approx 2.02\;\text{s}.$$

What does “2.02 s” mean? It tells us that, ignoring air resistance, an object dropped from a 20‑meter balcony will reach the ground just after two seconds. This is a concrete statement we can compare with a real‑world stopwatch. If the answer had been $0.02\,$s, we would suspect a slip in the algebra because a human cannot fall that fast from that height.

> **In daily life:** When a recipe says “bake for 15 minutes”, the number is only useful if we also know the unit (minutes). Forgetting the unit would make the instruction meaningless.

### 3. Explore how changing parameters affects the outcome

#### Changing gravity

If the same drop occurred on the Moon, where $g_{\text{moon}}\approx1.6\,$m/s\(^2\), the time becomes

$$t_{\text{moon}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\cdot20}{1.6}} \approx 5.0\;\text{s}.$$

The lower gravity makes the fall slower, roughly 2.5 times longer. This shows the formula’s sensitivity: $t$ grows like $1/\sqrt{g}$.

#### Changing the growth rate in the logistic model

For the logistic population model $P(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ae^{-rt}}$, the parameter $r$ is the intrinsic growth rate. If $r$ doubles, the exponent $-rt$ halves in magnitude for a given $t$, making $e^{-rt}$ smaller and $P(t)$ larger. In plain words, the population reaches its carrying capacity faster.

#### Changing price in consumer surplus

Consumer surplus is the area between the demand curve and the market price. If the market price rises from $p_1$ to $p_2$, the surplus shrinks by the rectangle of width $(p_2-p_1)$ and height equal to the quantity demanded at $p_1$. Numerically, a $5\,$dollar increase might cut the surplus from $200$ dollars to $150$ dollars, indicating that buyers are now less “happy” with the purchase.

> **Remember:** After any calculation, ask yourself: *What are the units?* *What does the number describe?* *If I change a key input, how does the answer move?* Answering these three questions turns a raw number into useful knowledge.

### Quick checklist for verification

1. Write down the units of every variable before substituting numbers.  
2. Perform the algebra, then simplify the units; they should match the quantity you are solving for.  
3. State the result in a full sentence that explains its meaning.  
4. Change one parameter slightly (e.g., increase $g$ by 10 %) and recompute to see the direction of change.  

By habitually applying this checklist, you develop confidence that your models not only solve equations but also describe the real world accurately.

sections.heading: 6. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
sections.body:
When you turn a word problem into a mathematical model, the smallest slip can change the whole answer. Below are the most frequent mistakes students make and simple ways to catch them before they spoil your work.

> **Common mistake:** *Mixing up dependent and independent variables*  
The **dependent variable** is the quantity that changes **because of** something else; the **independent variable** is the thing you control or that progresses naturally (often time).  
If you write the height of a falling ball as $h(t)=\frac12gt^2$ you have swapped the roles: height depends on time, not the other way around. The correct model is  
$$h(t)=h_0-\frac12gt^2,$$  
where $h_0$ is the initial height (a constant). Always ask: *What am I solving for?* If the answer is “height,” then height must be the dependent variable, written as a function of the independent variable $t$.

> **Remember:** *Write the variable you are solving for as a function of the independent variable.*  
A quick check: replace the independent variable with a number (e.g., $t=2$ seconds). The expression should give you a single, sensible value for the dependent variable (e.g., a height in meters). If it gives a time instead, you have the variables reversed.

> **Common mistake:** *Forgetting constants of integration*  
When you integrate a rate, you are essentially “undoing” a derivative. The antiderivative is never unique; it always includes a **constant of integration** (usually written $C$).  
For example, if the velocity of a car is $v(t)=3t$, the distance traveled is  
$$s(t)=\int 3t\,dt = \frac32 t^2 + C.$$  
If you drop the $+C$, you assume the car started at the origin, which may be false. The constant is determined by an **initial condition**, such as “the car was 5 m from the start line at $t=0$.” Plugging $t=0$ gives $5 = C$, so the full model becomes $s(t)=\frac32 t^2 + 5$.

> **Note:** *Always write “+ C” after an indefinite integral, then use given data to find $C$.*  
A handy mental shortcut: after each integration step, pause and ask, “Did the problem tell me where the object started or how much was present at the beginning?” If yes, that information will fix the constant.

> **Common mistake:** *Misreading the problem statement*  
Word problems often hide crucial details in plain language. Phrases like “after 5 seconds,” “per unit time,” or “when the population reaches 1000” are not decorative; they tell you **when** to evaluate your model or **what** value to set as a condition.  
Consider the logistic growth model for a bacteria culture:  
$$P(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ae^{-rt}},$$  
where $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$, $K$ is the carrying capacity, $r$ is the growth rate, and $A$ is a constant determined by the initial population $P(0)$. If the problem says “the culture starts with 200 cells and the carrying capacity is 5000,” you must use $P(0)=200$ to find $A$:
$$200=\frac{5000}{1+A}\;\Longrightarrow\;A=24.$$  
Skipping this step and using $A=1$ would give a completely wrong curve.

> **In daily life:** *Think of a recipe.* The instructions (problem statement) tell you how much flour, sugar, and butter to add **before** you start mixing. If you ignore “add 2 cups of flour” and just mix whatever you have, the cake will not turn out as expected. Similarly, every number or condition in a word problem is an ingredient for the correct mathematical “recipe.”

**How to avoid these pitfalls**

1. **Identify variables first.** Write a short list:  
   - Independent variable (usually $t$ for time).  
   - Dependent variable (the quantity you need to find).  
   - Parameters (constants like $g$, $K$, or $r$).  

2. **Translate each sentence.** After reading a clause, write the corresponding mathematical piece next to it. For example, “the object falls 5 m in the first second” becomes $h(1)=h_0-\frac12g(1)^2=5$.

3. **Mark every integration.** Immediately write “$+C$” and note where you will later substitute an initial condition.

4. **Check units and logic.** Plug in simple numbers (e.g., $t=0$) to see if the model gives a realistic value (height should be the initial height, not zero unless the object starts at ground level).

By following these small, systematic steps, you turn a confusing word problem into a clear, reliable mathematical model, and you keep the common errors from sneaking in unnoticed.

sections.heading: 7. Practice Problems and Reflection
sections.body:
Think of each problem as a short story.  
First read the story, then decide what the unknown quantity is, write an equation that describes the situation, and finally solve it.  
After you finish, answer the reflection questions to see how well you turned the word problem into a mathematical model.

---

**Problem 1 – Physics (Free‑fall)**  

A ball is dropped from a height of $120\ \text{m}$ above the ground.  
Air resistance is negligible and the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.  

*Task:*  
1. Write a function $s(t)$ that gives the height of the ball $t$ seconds after it is released.  
2. Find the time $t$ when the ball hits the ground.  

*Steps you might follow*  
- Let $s(t)$ be the height (in meters) at time $t$ (seconds).  
- Because the ball starts from rest, its initial velocity $v_0=0$.  
- The position of an object under constant acceleration $a$ is  
$$ s(t)=s_0+v_0 t+\tfrac12 a t^2 $$  
where $s_0$ is the initial height.  
- Set $s(t)=0$ (ground level) and solve for $t$.

---

**Problem 2 – Biology (Logistic growth)**  

A small lake contains a fish population that follows the logistic model  
$$ P(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ae^{-rt}} $$  
where $P(t)$ is the number of fish $t$ years after today, $K=10\,000$ is the carrying capacity (maximum sustainable population), $r=0.6\ \text{yr}^{-1}$ is the intrinsic growth rate, and $A$ is a constant determined by the initial population.  
Today the lake has $P(0)=2\,000$ fish.

*Task:*  
1. Find the value of $A$.  
2. Predict the population after $5$ years.  

*Steps you might follow*  
- Plug $t=0$ into the formula to get $P(0)=\frac{K}{1+A}$.  
- Solve this equation for $A$.  
- Then substitute $A$ and $t=5$ into the logistic formula to compute $P(5)$.

---

**Problem 3 – Economics (Consumer surplus)**  

The demand for a product is described by the price function $p(q)=120-0.5q$, where $p$ is the price in dollars and $q$ is the quantity demanded.  
The market price is fixed at $p=70$ dollars.

*Task:*  
1. Determine the quantity $q$ that consumers will buy at this price.  
2. Compute the consumer surplus, the area between the demand curve and the price line, from $q=0$ to the quantity found in part 1.  

*Steps you might follow*  
- Set $p(q)=70$ and solve for $q$.  
- Consumer surplus is the integral of the difference between the demand price and the market price:  
$$ \text{CS}= \int_{0}^{q^*}\bigl(p(q)-70\bigr)\,dq $$  
where $q^*$ is the quantity from part 1.  
- Evaluate the integral to obtain the surplus in dollars.

---

> **Note:** When you turn a word problem into a model, always identify the *variables* (what changes) and the *constants* (what stays fixed). This prevents mixing up units and makes the algebra easier.

> **Remember:** After solving, check that your answer makes sense in the original story. Does a time of $3$ seconds for a $120\,$m drop seem reasonable? Does a fish population of $9\,800$ after $5$ years look plausible given the carrying capacity?

> **In daily life:** Modeling is like making a recipe. The ingredients (numbers from the story) are measured, the cooking steps (equations) are followed, and the final dish (solution) is tasted to see if it matches what you expected.

### Reflection prompts  

1. **Identify the model:** For each problem, write a one‑sentence description of the real‑world situation you are modeling (e.g., “the height of a falling ball as a function of time”).  

2. **List assumptions:** Note any simplifications you made (e.g., “air resistance ignored”, “growth rate constant”). Why were they necessary?  

3. **Interpret the result:** Explain in plain language what the numerical answer tells you about the original situation.  

4. **Evaluate the model:** Could a different model give a more accurate picture? Suggest one possible improvement for each problem (e.g., adding a drag term for the falling ball).  

Answer these questions in a notebook or on a sheet of paper. Revisiting them later will help you see how mathematical modeling connects the abstract symbols to the concrete world.

examples.title: Falling stone height after 2 s
examples.given: A stone is dropped from rest. Find its height above the ground after $t=2\,$s.

steps.label: Define variables
steps.text: Let $h(t)$ be the height (m) and $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ the acceleration due to gravity.

steps.label: Write model
steps.text: Since the stone starts from rest, $h(t)=h_0-\frac12gt^2$, where $h_0$ is the initial height.

examples.answer: After 2 s the stone is $0.4\,$m above the ground.

examples.title: Logistic growth of a bacteria culture
examples.given: A bacteria population follows $P(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ae^{-rt}}$ with carrying capacity $K=10^6$, growth rate $r=0.8\ \text{day}^{-1}$, and $P(0)=10^4$. Find $P(5)$ (population after 5 days).
examples.answer: After 5 days the population is about $3.6\times10^5$ bacteria.

examples.title: Consumer surplus for a linear demand curve
examples.given: Demand: $p=120-2q$ (price $p$ in dollars, quantity $q$ in units). Supply: $p=20+q$. Find the consumer surplus at equilibrium.

steps.label: Sketch area
steps.text: Consumer surplus = area between demand curve and price line from $q=0$ to $q^*$.

steps.label: Compute area (triangle)
steps.text: Height = $p_{\text{max}}-p^*$ where $p_{\text{max}}$ is price when $q=0$: $p_{\text{max}}=120$. Height $=120-53.\overline{3}=66.\overline{6}$. Base $=q^*=33.\overline{3}$.

examples.answer: The consumer surplus at equilibrium is approximately $\$1{,}111$.

practice.q: A ball is dropped from a height of $20\,$m. Using $g=10\,$m/s², find the time it takes to hit the ground.
practice.a:
The height as a function of time is $s(t)=20-\frac12gt^2$. Set $s(t)=0$:
$$0=20-\frac12(10)t^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 5t^2=20 \;\Longrightarrow\; t^2=4 \;\Longrightarrow\; t=2\ \text{s}.$$

practice.q: A small fish population follows the logistic model with $r=0.6\,$day⁻¹ and carrying capacity $K=500$. If $P(0)=50$, find $P(5)$.
practice.a:
Logistic solution: $P(t)=\dfrac{K}{1+Ce^{-rt}}$.
First find $C$ using $P(0)=50$:
$$50=\frac{500}{1+C}\;\Longrightarrow\;1+C=10\;\Longrightarrow\;C=9.$$
Now compute $P(5)$:
$$P(5)=\frac{500}{1+9e^{-0.6\cdot5}}=\frac{500}{1+9e^{-3}}.$$
$e^{-3}\approx0.0498$, so denominator $=1+9(0.0498)\approx1+0.448=1.448$.
Thus $P(5)\approx\frac{500}{1.448}\approx345\,$ fish.

practice.q: A demand curve is $p=100-2q$. The market price is $p_0=40$. Compute the consumer surplus for the quantity sold.
practice.a:
First find $Q$ where $p=40$:
$$40=100-2Q \;\Longrightarrow\;2Q=60 \;\Longrightarrow\;Q=30.$$
Total willingness to pay:
$$\int_{0}^{30}(100-2q)\,dq = \Big[100q - q^2\Big]_{0}^{30}=100(30)-30^2=3000-900=2100.$$
Actual expenditure: $p_0 Q = 40 \times 30 = 1200$.
Consumer surplus $CS = 2100 - 1200 = 900$ (dollars).

practice.q: A tank drains water such that the rate of change of volume $V(t)$ satisfies $\displaystyle \frac{dV}{dt} = -k\sqrt{V}$, with $k=2\,$L$^{1/2}$/min. If the tank starts with $V(0)=16\,$L, find $V(5)$.
practice.a:
Separate variables:
$$\frac{dV}{\sqrt{V}} = -k\,dt.$$
Integrate:
$$\int V^{-1/2}\,dV = -k\int dt \;\Longrightarrow\; 2\sqrt{V} = -kt + C.$$
Use $V(0)=16$: $2\sqrt{16}=2\cdot4=8 = C$.
Thus $2\sqrt{V}= -2t + 8 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sqrt{V}=4 - t.$
Square both sides: $V=(4-t)^2$.
At $t=5$: $V=(4-5)^2 = (-1)^2 = 1\,$L.

practice.q: A particle moves along a line with acceleration $a(t)=6t-4$. Its initial velocity is $v(0)=3$ m/s and initial position $s(0)=2$ m. Find the position $s(t)$ and the time when the particle returns to $s=2$ m.
practice.a:
Integrate acceleration to get velocity:
$$v(t)=\int a(t)\,dt = \int (6t-4)\,dt = 3t^2-4t + C_1.$$
Use $v(0)=3$: $C_1=3$. So $v(t)=3t^2-4t+3$.
Integrate velocity to get position:
$$s(t)=\int v(t)\,dt = \int (3t^2-4t+3)\,dt = t^3-2t^2+3t + C_2.$$
Use $s(0)=2$: $C_2=2$. Hence $s(t)=t^3-2t^2+3t+2$.
Set $s(t)=2$ to find return time:
$$t^3-2t^2+3t+2 = 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; t^3-2t^2+3t =0.$$
Factor $t$: $t(t^2-2t+3)=0$.
Solutions: $t=0$ (the start) or $t^2-2t+3=0$.
Discriminant $(-2)^2-4\cdot1\cdot3 =4-12=-8<0$, no real roots.
Thus the particle never returns to $s=2$ after $t>0$.

practice.q: A company’s cost function is $C(q)=0.05q^3-0.6q^2+12q+100$, where $q$ is the number of units produced. Find the production level that minimizes average cost, and compute that minimum average cost.
practice.a:
Average cost $AC(q)=\dfrac{C(q)}{q}=0.05q^2-0.6q+12+\dfrac{100}{q}$.
To minimize, differentiate and set to zero:
$$\frac{d}{dq}AC(q)=0.10q-0.6-\frac{100}{q^2}=0.$$
Multiply by $q^2$: $0.10q^3-0.6q^2-100=0$.
Simplify: $q^3-6q^2-1000=0$ (multiply by 10).
We look for an integer root; test $q=10$: $1000-600-1000=-600\neq0$.
Test $q=20$: $8000-2400-1000=4600$.
Test $q=25$: $15625-3750-1000=10875$.
Use trial $q=...$ Use rational root theorem: possible roots $\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm5,\pm8,\pm10,\pm20,\pm25,\pm40,\pm50,\pm100$. Test $q=...$
Try $q=...$ Actually we can solve numerically. Let $f(q)=0.10q-0.6-100/q^2$. Use iteration:
Start $q=5$: $0.5-0.6-4= -4.1$ (negative).
$q=10$: $1-0.6-1= -0.6$ (negative).
$q=12$: $1.2-0.6-0.694≈ -0.094$ (negative).
$q=13$: $1.3-0.6-0.593≈0.107$ (positive).
So root between 12 and 13. Linear interpolation:
At 12, $f=-0.094$; at 13, $f=0.107$. Approx root $q≈12+ \frac{0.094}{0.094+0.107}\approx12+0.467≈12.47$.
Thus minimizing production level $q\approx12.5$ units (round to nearest whole unit, $q=12$ or $13$).
Compute minimum average cost using $q=12.5$:
First compute $C(12.5)=0.05(12.5)^3-0.6(12.5)^2+12(12.5)+100$
$(12.5)^3=1953.125$, times $0.05$ = $97.6563$
$(12.5)^2=156.25$, times $0.6$ = $93.75$
$12(12.5)=150$
So $C=97.6563-93.75+150+100=253.9063$.
Average cost $AC= C/q = 253.9063/12.5 ≈20.31$ dollars per unit.
Therefore, the production level that minimizes average cost is about $12$–$13$ units, and the minimum average cost is roughly $\$20.3$ per unit.

data.recap: This lesson shows how to turn real‑world stories into mathematical models by picking the right variables and writing equations. It walks through examples from physics (free fall), biology (logistic growth), and economics (consumer surplus) and stresses checking units and interpretation. Finally, it lists common mistakes and gives practice problems to reinforce the modelling steps.

key_terms.meaning: A symbol that represents a quantity that can change.
The quantity that is controlled or progresses naturally, often time.
The quantity that changes because of the independent variable.
The instantaneous rate of change of a function.
The sum of many tiny pieces to find a total amount.
The maximum population an environment can sustain indefinitely.
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay.
Labels that tell what a number measures, such as meters or seconds.

quiz.q: What is the first step when modelling a word problem?
quiz.why: Identifying the variable captures the changing quantity you need to solve for.

quiz.q: In a free‑fall problem, which variable is typically independent?
quiz.why: Time progresses naturally and is used as the independent variable.

quiz.q: What does the derivative of a position function represent?
quiz.why: The derivative of position with respect to time gives instantaneous velocity.

quiz.q: In the logistic population model, what does the symbol K stand for?
quiz.why: K is defined as the carrying capacity, the maximum sustainable population.

quiz.q: Which expression gives the consumer surplus for a linear demand q(p)=a-bp and market price p0?

integral from p0 to a/b of (a-bp) dp
quiz.why: Consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve above the market price, from p0 up to the intercept a/b.

quiz.q: When checking a result, which of the following is NOT a recommended step?

quiz.why: Ignoring the sign can hide errors; checking units, interpretation, and sensitivity are all recommended.
