lessons.title: and integrals to real‑world problems in physics

data.title: and integrals to real‑world problems in physics
data.summary: In this lesson students learn how to apply limits, derivatives, and integrals to solve real‑world physics problems. They will see step‑by‑step examples that connect calculus concepts to motion, forces, and energy.
objectives: Apply limits to describe instantaneous velocity and acceleration
Differentiate position functions to find velocity and acceleration
Integrate acceleration to recover velocity and position
Set up and evaluate definite integrals for work and energy
Interpret the physical meaning of calculus results
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand limits, derivatives, basic integration techniques, and how to compute definite integrals.
why: Physics relies on calculus to model how objects move and interact; without these tools we cannot predict trajectories, forces, or energy changes.
Being able to translate a real situation into a mathematical model builds problem‑solving confidence and prepares students for engineering, biology, and economics applications.

sections.heading: 1. Review of Key Calculus Tools
sections.body:
When we talk about “instantaneous” quantities in physics, we are asking for the value of something at a single moment, just as a photograph captures a single instant. Calculus gives us a precise way to find that value by looking at what happens in a very, very short time interval.

> **Definition:** The *instantaneous rate of change* of a function $f(t)$ at a time $t_0$ is the limit  

$$\displaystyle \lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{f(t_0+\Delta t)-f(t_0)}{\Delta t}.$$  

This limit is called the **derivative** of $f$ at $t_0$, written $f'(t_0)$ or $\dfrac{df}{dt}(t_0)$.  

In words, we take the average rate of change over a small interval $\Delta t$, then shrink that interval until it is almost zero. The number that the fraction approaches is the exact rate at that instant.

Why does this work? Imagine driving a car and looking at the speedometer. The speedometer does not show the average speed over the last hour; it shows how fast the car is moving right now. The speedometer is essentially performing the limit operation on the distance‑versus‑time graph: it measures the slope of the curve at the point where the needle points.

The derivative also has a geometric meaning: it is the **slope** of the tangent line to the graph of $f(t)$ at the point $(t_0,f(t_0))$. A tangent line just touches the curve without cutting through it, matching the curve’s direction at that point. If the curve is steep, the slope (and therefore the derivative) is large; if the curve is flat, the slope is near zero.

> **In daily life:** Think of a hill. The steepness of the hill at any spot tells you how hard it is to walk there. The steeper the hill, the larger the slope. The derivative tells you that steepness for any curve, not just a hill.

---

### Antiderivative – Reversing the Process

If a derivative tells us “how fast,” an **antiderivative** tells us “how much total.” Formally, a function $F(t)$ is an antiderivative of $f(t)$ if  

$$\displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}F(t)=f(t).$$  

Geometrically, $F(t)$ measures the **area under the curve** of $f$ from a fixed starting point up to $t$. This is the idea behind the definite integral:

$$\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b} f(t)\,dt = \text{area under }f(t)\text{ from }t=a\text{ to }t=b.$$

The integral adds up infinitely many tiny rectangles of width $\Delta t$ and height $f(t)$, just as you would add up the slices of a loaf of bread to find the whole loaf’s volume.

> **Note:** The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the two ideas: the derivative of an integral returns the original function, and the integral of a derivative gives the net change between two points.

---

### Example: A Falling Object

Suppose a ball is dropped from a height and its position (measured upward from the ground) is given by  

$$s(t)=100-4.9t^{2},$$  

where $s$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds.  

1. **Velocity** – the instantaneous rate of change of position:  

$$v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}= -9.8t.$$  

At $t=2\,$s, $v(2)=-19.6\,$m/s, meaning the ball is moving downward at $19.6\,$m/s.

2. **Acceleration** – the rate of change of velocity:  

$$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}= -9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}.$$  

The acceleration is constant; gravity pulls the ball downward with the same strength at every moment.

3. **Distance fallen** – the total distance the ball has traveled after $t$ seconds is the integral of speed (the absolute value of velocity). Since the ball starts from rest and moves downward, we can integrate the speed $|v(t)|=9.8t$:  

$$\displaystyle \int_{0}^{t}9.8\tau\,d\tau = 4.9t^{2}.$$

Notice that this is exactly the drop in height $100-s(t)$, confirming that the antiderivative recovers the original position change.

> **Remember:** Derivative = “instantaneous change” (slope). Antiderivative = “total accumulated change” (area). Both are tools for turning a picture of motion into numbers we can predict and compare.

sections.heading: 2. Motion Problems – From Position to Velocity to Acceleration
sections.body:
When we talk about **motion** we want to know how an object’s position changes over time.  
Suppose we have a function $s(t)$ that tells us the position (in meters) of a car at any time $t$ (in seconds).  
The first question we ask is: *how fast is the car moving right now?*  

> **Definition:** The **velocity** $v(t)$ is the rate at which position changes with time.  
> Mathematically, $v(t)$ is the derivative of $s(t)$ with respect to $t$:  

$$v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$$  

The derivative $\frac{ds}{dt}$ means “the tiny change in $s$ divided by the tiny change in $t$”.  
If $s$ increases a little when $t$ increases a little, the quotient is positive, so the velocity points in the positive direction.  

**Why it is useful:** Knowing $v(t)$ lets us predict where the car will be a short time later, because we know its instantaneous speed and direction.

---

### From position to velocity: a step‑by‑step example  

Imagine the car’s position is given by  

$$s(t)=5t^{2}+2\; \text{(meters)}$$  

1. **Identify the rule**: $s(t)=5t^{2}+2$.  
2. **Differentiate**: Apply the power rule $\frac{d}{dt}(t^{n})=n t^{\,n-1}$.  

$$v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(5t^{2}+2)=5\cdot2t^{1}+0=10t\; \text{(m/s)}$$  

The constant $2$ disappears because its derivative is $0$ (a constant does not change).  
Now we can read the velocity at any moment: at $t=3\,$s, $v(3)=10\cdot3=30\,$m/s.

> **In daily life:** This is like watching a runner on a track. The runner’s position $s(t)$ tells you where they are; the slope of the position curve at a particular instant tells you how fast they are running right then.

---

### Acceleration: the change of velocity  

Just as velocity tells us “how fast position changes”, **acceleration** tells us “how fast velocity changes”.  

> **Definition:** The **acceleration** $a(t)$ is the derivative of velocity with respect to time, or the second derivative of position:  

$$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}}$$  

The unit of $a(t)$ is meters per second squared (m/s²), meaning “meters per second, each second”.

Continuing the example:

$$a(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(10t)=10\; \text{(m/s}^{2}\text{)}$$  

Here the acceleration is constant: the car’s speed increases by $10\,$m/s every second.

> **Note:** A constant acceleration is what you see when an object falls near Earth’s surface (ignoring air resistance). The acceleration is about $9.8\,$m/s² downward.

---

### Interpreting the numbers  

- **Position $s(t)$** tells *where* the object is.  
- **Velocity $v(t)$** tells *how fast* and *in which direction* it is moving at that instant.  
- **Acceleration $a(t)$** tells *whether the speed is increasing or decreasing* and *how quickly*.

If $v(t)$ is positive, the object moves in the positive $s$‑direction; if $v(t)$ is negative, it moves opposite.  
If $a(t)$ is positive while $v(t)$ is positive, the object speeds up.  
If $a(t)$ is negative while $v(t)$ is positive, the object slows down (decelerates).

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the derivative gives an *instantaneous* rate, not an average over a time interval. For example, the average speed from $t=0$ to $t=2$ s is $(s(2)-s(0))/2$, which is different from $v(1)$, the speed exactly at $t=1$ s.

---

### Quick checklist for converting $s(t)$ → $v(t)$ → $a(t)$  

1. Write down the position function with correct units.  
2. Differentiate once to get $v(t)$; attach units of m/s.  
3. Differentiate again to get $a(t)$; attach units of m/s².  
4. Plug in the time of interest to interpret the physical meaning.

> **Remember:** Differentiation is just “finding the slope” of the curve at a point. The slope tells you the instantaneous rate of change, which in motion becomes velocity and then acceleration.

sections.heading: 3. Limits for Instantaneous Quantities
sections.body:
When we talk about “instantaneous” quantities we mean the value at a single instant, not an average over a period of time.  
For a moving object the **instantaneous velocity** at time $t$ is the slope of the curve that shows its position $s(t)$ versus time.  
That slope is the same as the slope of the line that just touches the curve at the point $(t,\,s(t))$ – the **tangent line**.

> **Definition:** The instantaneous velocity $v(t)$ is the limit of the average velocity over a shrinking time interval:
> $$v(t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

Why does this work?  
Imagine you measure how far a car travels in 1 second, then in 0.5 seconds, then in 0.1 seconds, and so on. Each measurement gives an **average velocity** for that short interval:
$$\text{average velocity}=\frac{\text{change in position}}{\text{change in time}}=\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}.$$
If we keep making the interval shorter, the average velocity gets closer to the true speed at the exact moment $t$. The limit captures this idea mathematically.

### Step‑by‑step computation

1. **Write the position function.**  
   Suppose a ball is dropped from a height and its height (in meters) after $t$ seconds is described by  
   $$s(t)=9.8t^2-5t^3.$$
   This function is smooth, but the cubic term makes the derivative a bit messy, so we will use the limit definition instead of memorising the rule.

2. **Form the difference quotient.**  
   Replace $t$ by $t+\Delta t$ and subtract $s(t)$:
   \[
   s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)=9.8(t+\Delta t)^2-5(t+\Delta t)^3-\bigl(9.8t^2-5t^3\bigr).
   \]

3. **Expand and simplify.**  
   Expand each power, keep terms up to $\Delta t$, and factor out $\Delta t$:
   \[
   s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)=\Delta t\bigl(19.6t-15t^2\bigr)+\Delta t^2\bigl(9.8-15t\bigr)-5\Delta t^3.
   \]

4. **Divide by $\Delta t$.**  
   $$\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}=19.6t-15t^2+\Delta t\bigl(9.8-15t\bigr)-5\Delta t^2.$$

5. **Take the limit as $\Delta t\to0$.**  
   All terms containing $\Delta t$ vanish, leaving
   $$v(t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{s(t+\Delta t)-s(t)}{\Delta t}=19.6t-15t^2.$$

   This is the instantaneous velocity at any time $t$.

> **In daily life:** Think of a speedometer in a car. It does not show the average speed over the last minute; it shows the speed at the exact moment you look at it. The speedometer is essentially performing the limit process inside the car’s computer.

### Connecting to the tangent line

The equation of the tangent line at time $t_0$ can be written as
$$y = s(t_0) + v(t_0)(t-t_0).$$
Here $v(t_0)$ is the slope we just found. The line touches the curve at $(t_0, s(t_0))$ and has the same instantaneous direction as the curve there. If you draw the curve and the line together, the line will just “kiss” the curve without crossing it nearby.

> **Note:** The limit definition works even when the function is not differentiable in the usual algebraic sense (for example, a piecewise‑defined position). As long as the limit exists, the instantaneous velocity is well defined.

### Why limits matter in physics

Many physical formulas involve rates that change continuously – acceleration, electric current, heat flow. Using limits lets us turn a messy average over a tiny interval into a precise instantaneous value, which is the foundation of differential equations that describe motion, growth, and decay.

> **Remember:** Always start from the difference quotient, simplify, and then let the interval shrink to zero. If any term still contains $\Delta t$ after you take the limit, you have made a mistake in algebra.

### Quick check

- Write the average velocity for the interval $[2,\,2+\Delta t]$ using $s(t)=9.8t^2-5t^3$.
- Simplify, divide by $\Delta t$, and let $\Delta t\to0$.
- Verify that you obtain $v(2)=19.6(2)-15(2)^2 = 39.2-60 = -20.8\ \text{m/s}$.

If you get a different number, revisit the algebraic expansion – that is a common source of error.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to cancel the $\Delta t$ factor before taking the limit. The limit of $\Delta t$ itself is zero, which would incorrectly give $v(t)=0$.

By mastering this limit process you gain a reliable tool for finding instantaneous velocities (and later accelerations) even when the function looks intimidating. This skill bridges the gap between the smooth world of calculus and the real‑world measurements engineers and physicists rely on every day.

sections.heading: 4. Work and Energy – Definite Integrals
sections.body:
When a force pulls or pushes an object while it moves, the force can give the object energy.  
The amount of energy transferred is called **work**.  Work is the sum of tiny pieces of force acting over tiny pieces of distance.  If the force changes with position, we cannot just multiply “force × distance”; we must add up all the little contributions.  This addition is exactly what a **definite integral** does.

> **Definition:** *Work* $W$ is the integral of the force component along the direction of motion, written $W=\displaystyle\int_{x_i}^{x_f} \mathbf{F}(x)\cdot d\mathbf{x}$.

Here  

* $\mathbf{F}(x)$ is the force vector at position $x$ (the force may vary).  
* $d\mathbf{x}$ is an infinitesimal displacement vector pointing in the direction of motion.  
* The dot product $\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{x}$ picks out the component of the force that actually pushes the object forward.  
* $x_i$ and $x_f$ are the starting and ending positions.

If the motion is along a straight line and the force points along that line, the dot product reduces to ordinary multiplication, and we can write the scalar form  

$$
W=\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx .
$$

### Why the integral gives the correct energy

Imagine the path broken into many tiny segments of length $\Delta x$.  On each segment the force is almost constant, so the work on that piece is approximately $F(x_k)\,\Delta x$.  Adding all pieces gives  

$$
\sum_{k}F(x_k)\,\Delta x .
$$

When we let the segment length become infinitely small, the sum becomes the integral $\int F(x)\,dx$.  The limit process guarantees that we have accounted for every tiny change in force, no matter how quickly it varies.

### Example: Stretching a spring

A spring obeys Hooke’s law: $F(x)=k\,x$, where $k$ is the spring constant and $x$ is the displacement from the relaxed length.  Suppose we stretch the spring from $x=0$ to $x=0.5\,$m.  The work done is  

$$
W=\int_{0}^{0.5} k\,x\,dx .
$$

To evaluate, we find an **antiderivative** (a function whose derivative is the integrand).  The antiderivative of $k\,x$ is $\frac12 k x^{2}$, because  

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\!\left(\frac12 k x^{2}\right)=k x .
$$

Now apply the **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus**, which tells us to subtract the antiderivative at the lower limit from its value at the upper limit:

$$
W=\left[\frac12 k x^{2}\right]_{0}^{0.5}
   =\frac12 k (0.5)^{2}-\frac12 k (0)^{2}
   =\frac12 k \times 0.25
   =0.125\,k .
$$

If $k=200\,$N/m, then $W=0.125\times200=25\,$J (joules).  This number means that 25 J of energy have been stored in the spring as **potential energy**.

> **In daily life:** Stretching a rubber band, compressing a car’s shock absorber, or pulling a sled up a hill all involve work calculated by an integral when the force is not constant.

### Interpreting the result

The value of $W$ tells us how much energy moved from the person (or motor) doing the pulling into the object being moved.  If the force is conservative (like a spring or gravity), the work equals the change in a stored energy form (potential energy).  If the force is non‑conservative (like friction), the work appears as thermal energy.

> **Remember:** The limits $x_i$ and $x_f$ must match the direction of motion.  Reversing them changes the sign of $W$, indicating that energy is taken out of the system instead of put in.

### Common mistake to avoid

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting the dot product when the force is not parallel to the motion.  Using $F\,dx$ without checking direction can give a wrong magnitude or even the wrong sign.

### Quick checklist for solving a work problem

1. Identify the direction of motion and express the force component along that direction, $F(x)$.  
2. Write the integral $W=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}F(x)\,dx$.  
3. Find an antiderivative of $F(x)$.  
4. Evaluate it at the upper and lower limits and subtract.  
5. State the physical meaning of the sign and magnitude of $W$.

By following these steps, you turn a variable force into a precise amount of energy transferred, ready to be used in further physics calculations such as kinetic energy, power, or conservation‑of‑energy problems.

sections.heading: 5. Solving Real‑World Problems Step‑by‑Step
sections.body:
Imagine a car that starts from rest and a engine that pushes harder when the car is slow, but the push gets weaker as the car speeds up.  To find how far the car travels in a given time we must **combine** three ideas we have already met:

1. **Limits** – to turn an average speed into an instantaneous speed.  
2. **Derivatives** – to describe how a quantity (speed) changes with another (time).  
3. **Integrals** – to add up tiny pieces of distance over time.

> **Definition:** *Instantaneous velocity* $v(t)$ is the limit of the average velocity $\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$ as the time interval $\Delta t$ becomes infinitesimally small.

---

### Step 1 – Write the force law

Suppose the engine produces a force that depends on the current speed $v$:

$$F(v)=F_0 - k\,v,$$

where $F_0$ (newtons) is the maximum force when the car is at rest, and $k$ (newtons·seconds/meter) measures how quickly the force drops as speed grows.  This kind of “drag‑like” force appears in real cars because air resistance grows with speed.

> **In daily life:** Think of trying to push a stroller uphill; the harder you push, the faster you go, but the hill (air resistance) pushes back harder the faster you move.

---

### Step 2 – Relate force to acceleration

Newton’s second law tells us that force equals mass times acceleration:

$$F = m\,a,$$

with $m$ the car’s mass (kilograms) and $a$ the acceleration (meters per second squared).  Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:

$$a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}.$$

Insert the force law:

$$m\,\frac{dv}{dt}=F_0 - k\,v.$$

---

### Step 3 – Solve the differential equation for $v(t)$

We have a first‑order linear differential equation.  Separate the variables:

$$\frac{dv}{F_0 - k\,v}= \frac{dt}{m}.$$

Integrate both sides.  The left side needs a *limit* because the denominator becomes zero when $v=F_0/k$, but our car never reaches that speed in the short time we consider, so the integral is well‑defined.

$$\int_{0}^{v(t)}\frac{dv}{F_0 - k\,v}= \int_{0}^{t}\frac{dt}{m}.$$

The integral on the left is a standard form:

$$-\frac{1}{k}\ln\!\bigl(F_0 - k\,v\bigr)\Big|_{0}^{v(t)} = \frac{t}{m}.$$

Evaluating the limits:

$$-\frac{1}{k}\Bigl[\ln\!\bigl(F_0 - k\,v(t)\bigr)-\ln(F_0)\Bigr]=\frac{t}{m}.$$

Multiply by $-k$ and exponentiate:

$$\ln\!\frac{F_0 - k\,v(t)}{F_0}= -\frac{k}{m}t,$$

$$\frac{F_0 - k\,v(t)}{F_0}= e^{-\frac{k}{m}t},$$

$$v(t)=\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl(1-e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}\Bigr).$$

So the car’s speed starts at $0$ and approaches the limiting speed $F_0/k$ as $t$ grows.

---

### Step 4 – Find the distance traveled

Distance $s(t)$ is the integral of velocity:

$$s(t)=\int_{0}^{t} v(\tau)\,d\tau.$$

Insert $v(\tau)$:

$$s(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl(1-e^{-\frac{k}{m}\tau}\Bigr)d\tau.$$

Separate the integral:

$$s(t)=\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl[\int_{0}^{t}1\,d\tau-\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\frac{k}{m}\tau}d\tau\Bigr].$$

The first integral is simply $t$.  The second integral uses the rule $\int e^{a\tau}d\tau=\frac{1}{a}e^{a\tau}$:

$$\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\frac{k}{m}\tau}d\tau=
\left[-\frac{m}{k}e^{-\frac{k}{m}\tau}\right]_{0}^{t}
=\frac{m}{k}\bigl(1-e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}\bigr).$$

Putting everything together:

$$s(t)=\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl[t-\frac{m}{k}\bigl(1-e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}\bigr)\Bigr].$$

This formula tells us exactly how far the car has moved after any time $t$.

> **Remember:** The distance comes from *integrating* velocity, just as velocity comes from *integrating* acceleration.  Each step adds up tiny pieces.

---

### Step 5 – Check the result

A quick sanity check: when $t\to0$, the exponential term $e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}\approx 1-\frac{k}{m}t$, so

$$s(t)\approx\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl[t-\frac{m}{k}\bigl(1-(1-\frac{k}{m}t)\bigr)\Bigr]
=\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl[t-\frac{m}{k}\cdot\frac{k}{m}t\Bigr]=0,$$

as expected—the car has not moved at the instant it starts.  For large $t$, the exponential term vanishes and

$$s(t)\approx\frac{F_0}{k}\Bigl[t-\frac{m}{k}\Bigr],$$

showing a nearly linear growth, which matches the intuition that once the car reaches its limiting speed, it travels almost uniformly.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to apply the limits when evaluating an integral.  Always plug in the lower and upper bounds; otherwise you may lose the constant that guarantees $s(0)=0$.

By following these five small steps—write the physical law, turn it into a differential equation, solve for the instantaneous quantity, integrate to get the accumulated quantity, and finally check—you can tackle many real‑world calculus problems, from cars on a road to rockets soaring through the sky.

sections.heading: 6. Common Pitfalls and Checks
sections.body:
When you finish a calculus problem in physics, the answer is not just a number – it must also make sense in the real world.  
The easiest ways to catch mistakes are to **check the units**, **look at the sign**, and **compare with physical intuition**.  
Each of these checks is a simple test you can do before you hand in your work.

> **Definition:** *Units* are the labels attached to a quantity, such as meters (m) for distance, seconds (s) for time, or joules (J) for energy.  
> **Note:** A correct answer must have the same units that the problem asks for.

### 1. Checking Units Step‑by‑Step  

1. **Write down the unit for every symbol** you use.  
   - If $x(t)$ is a position, write $[x]=\text{m}$.  
   - If $v(t)=\frac{dx}{dt}$, then $[v]=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$.  
   - If $a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}$, then $[a]=\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}$.

2. **Multiply or divide units exactly as you do numbers** when you apply formulas.  
   For example, the work done by a constant force $F$ over a distance $d$ is  

   $$
   W = F\,d
   $$  

   If $[F]=\text{N}$ (newtons) and $[d]=\text{m}$, then  

   $[W]=\text{N}\cdot\text{m} = \text{J}$ (joules).  

3. **After every integration or differentiation, verify the resulting unit**.  
   - An integral $\int v(t)\,dt$ adds a factor of time, so the unit becomes $\text{m/s}\times\text{s}= \text{m}$, which is a distance – exactly what you expect for a displacement.  
   - A derivative $\frac{d}{dt}( \frac12 mv^2 )$ introduces $1/\text{s}$, turning energy (J) into power (J/s), which is the unit of a rate of energy use.

If the final unit does not match what the problem asks for, you have likely misplaced a factor of $t$, $v$, or a constant.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include the unit of a constant (like $g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$) when integrating a force. The result will have the wrong unit, often revealing a missing $\,\text{s}$ or $\,\text{m}$.

### 2. Looking at the Sign  

Physical quantities often have a direction. In one‑dimensional motion, we choose a positive direction (rightward, upward, etc.).  

- **Velocity** is positive when the object moves in the chosen direction, negative otherwise.  
- **Work** is positive if the force and displacement point the same way, negative if they oppose each other.  

When you obtain a result, ask: *Does the sign agree with the situation?*  

Example: A block slides down a frictionless incline of height $h$. The gravitational potential energy lost is $mgh$, a positive number. The work done by gravity should also be positive because gravity pulls the block in the same direction as the motion. If your calculation gives $W = -mgh$, you have likely taken the displacement vector opposite to the force vector.

> **Remember:** A sign error often appears as a negative answer where a physical quantity cannot be negative (e.g., negative mass, negative distance). Use the sign to spot such slips quickly.

### 3. Using Physical Intuition  

Even if the units and sign are correct, the magnitude might be unreasonable. Ask yourself simple “what‑if” questions:

- **Order of magnitude:** If a car accelerates from $0$ to $20\ \text{m/s}$ in $5\ \text{s}$, the average acceleration is $4\ \text{m/s}^2$. If your calculation gives $400\ \text{m/s}^2$, something is off.  
- **Limiting cases:** Set a variable to $0$ or to a very large value and see what the formula predicts.  
  - For the kinetic energy $K=\frac12 mv^2$, if $v=0$ the energy must be $0$.  
  - For the work done by a constant force $F$ over distance $d$, if $d=0$ the work must be $0$.

- **Everyday comparison:** Compare the result to familiar numbers.  
  - Lifting a 1‑kg book one meter requires about $10\ \text{J}$ of work (since $g\approx10\ \text{m/s}^2$).  
  - If you compute $10^6\ \text{J}$ for the same task, you know the answer is far too large.

> **In daily life:** Think of a water faucet. The flow rate (volume per second) is analogous to a velocity, and the total volume collected after a minute is the integral of that flow rate. If you measured a flow of $2\ \text{L/s}$ but calculated $120\ \text{L}$ after one minute, you missed a factor of $60$ seconds – a classic unit‑check error.

### 4. A Quick Checklist Before You Finish  

1. **Units:** Write the unit of the final answer; does it match the question?  
2. **Sign:** Does the sign agree with the direction you chose?  
3. **Magnitude:** Is the number roughly what you expect from everyday experience or a limiting case?  
4. **Logic:** Does each step follow the previous one without skipping a factor (like forgetting a $1/2$ in kinetic energy)?

By habitually applying these four simple checks, you turn a long algebraic manipulation into a reliable, error‑resistant solution. The math will still be there, but now it is anchored firmly in the physical world you can see and feel.

sections.heading: 7. Practice and Reflection
sections.body:
> **Remember:** Practice is the bridge between understanding a concept and being able to use it confidently in new situations.

When you finish a problem, take a moment to translate the symbols back into words.  Explain *why* each step makes sense, not just *how* you did it.  This habit helps you see the physics behind the math and catches mistakes before they hide in algebra.

---

### Problem 1 – Falling ball  

A ball is dropped from a height of $20\,$m. Its height above the ground after $t$ seconds is given by  

$$h(t)=20-4.9t^{2}.$$  

1. Find the instantaneous velocity at $t=1.2\,$s by using the limit definition of the derivative.  
2. Write a short paragraph (2–3 sentences) describing what this velocity tells you about the ball’s motion at that instant.

*Hint:* The instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity over a short time interval:  

$$v(t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\frac{h(t+\Delta t)-h(t)}{\Delta t}.$$

---

### Problem 2 – Car accelerating  

A car’s position along a straight road (in meters) is modeled by  

$$s(t)=3t^{3}-12t^{2}+9t,$$  

where $t$ is measured in seconds.  

1. Compute the acceleration at $t=2\,$s by first finding the velocity $v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}$ and then the acceleration $a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}$.  
2. In a few sentences, explain how acceleration relates to the change in the car’s speed and direction at that moment.

*Remember:* Differentiation turns a position function into a velocity function, and a second differentiation gives acceleration.

---

### Problem 3 – Work done by a variable force  

A spring exerts a force $F(x)=kx$ on a block, where $k=8\,$N/m and $x$ is the displacement from the equilibrium position (in meters). The block is moved from $x=0$ to $x=0.5\,$m.  

1. Set up the definite integral that represents the total work done on the block.  
2. Evaluate the integral to find the work (in joules).  

Write a brief explanation of why the integral adds up “tiny pieces” of force over each tiny piece of distance.

*Note:* Work is the area under the force‑versus‑displacement curve:  

$$W=\int_{0}^{0.5} kx\,dx.$$

---

### Problem 4 – Power of a cyclist  

A cyclist pedals with a force that varies with time: $F(t)=10\sin(\pi t)$ newtons, applied over a distance that changes at a rate $v(t)=2t$ meters per second.  

1. Write an expression for the instantaneous power $P(t)$ (power = force × velocity).  
2. Compute the total energy expended from $t=0$ to $t=2\,$s by integrating the power function.  

Explain in words why multiplying force by velocity gives power, and why integrating power over time gives energy.

---

### Problem 5 – Reflective comparison  

Choose any two of the problems above. For each, answer the following prompts:

* **What was the main calculus tool you used?** (e.g., limit definition of derivative, definite integral)  
* **How did the physical meaning guide your mathematical steps?**  
* **If you changed a parameter (like the height in Problem 1 or the spring constant in Problem 3), how would the answer change qualitatively?**  

Write a short paragraph for each problem, focusing on the connection between the math operation and the physical concept.

---

> **In daily life:** When you check how fast a car is accelerating, you are essentially measuring how the speed changes in a very short time—exactly what a derivative tells us.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to include the units when interpreting a result.  Always write the final answer with its proper unit (m/s, J, etc.) and check that the units make sense.

By working through these problems and writing the explanations, you reinforce the idea that calculus is not just a collection of symbols, but a language that describes how things change in the real world.  Keep your reasoning clear, and the mathematics will follow naturally.

examples.title: Falling stone – velocity from position
examples.given: A stone is dropped from a height of $100\ \text{m}$. Its height as a function of time is $s(t)=100-4.9t^{2}$ (meters). Find its velocity after $2\ \text{s}$.

steps.label: Differentiate position
steps.text: Compute $v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}= -9.8t$ to get the velocity function.

examples.answer: The stone’s velocity after $2\ \text{s}$ is $-19.6\ \text{m/s}$ (downward).

examples.title: Car braking – distance from acceleration
examples.given: A car traveling at $20\ \text{m/s}$ applies brakes that produce a constant deceleration of $-4\ \text{m/s}^{2}$. Find the distance the car travels before stopping.

steps.label: Integrate to velocity
steps.text: $v(t)=\int a(t)\,dt = -4t + C$. Use $v(0)=20$ to get $C=20$, so $v(t)=20-4t$.

examples.answer: The car travels $50\ \text{m}$ before it comes to rest.

examples.title: Work done by a variable force on a spring
examples.given: A spring obeys Hooke’s law $F(x) = -kx$ with $k=200\ \text{N/m}$. It is compressed from its natural length $x=0$ to $x=0.1\ \text{m}$. Find the work done on the spring during this compression.

steps.label: Interpret sign
steps.text: Negative sign means the external agent does $+1\ \text{J}$ of work on the spring (energy stored).

examples.answer: The work required to compress the spring $0.1\ \text{m}$ is $1\ \text{J}$ (energy stored in the spring).

practice.q: A car moves along a straight road with position given by $s(t)=4t^{2}+2t$ meters, where $t$ is time in seconds. Find the car’s velocity at $t=3\,$s.
practice.a: Velocity is the derivative of position: $v(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}=8t+2$. Plug $t=3$: $v(3)=8(3)+2=24+2=26\,$m/s.

practice.q: A particle’s velocity is $v(t)=5-2t$ m/s. At what time does the particle come to rest?
practice.a: Set $v(t)=0$: $5-2t=0\Rightarrow 2t=5\Rightarrow t=\frac{5}{2}=2.5\,$s.

practice.q: A stone is dropped from a height of 80 m. Its height above ground after $t$ seconds is $h(t)=80-4.9t^{2}$. Compute the work done by gravity as the stone falls to the ground. (Take $g=9.8\,$m/s² and mass $m=1\,$kg.)
practice.a:
Work by gravity $W=\int_{0}^{T} mg\,v(t)\,dt$, where $v(t)=\frac{dh}{dt}=-9.8t$. First find the impact time $T$ from $h(T)=0$: $80-4.9T^{2}=0\Rightarrow T^{2}= \frac{80}{4.9}\approx16.33\Rightarrow T\approx4.04\,$s.
Now $W=\int_{0}^{4.04} (1)(9.8)(-9.8t)\,dt = -9.8^{2}\int_{0}^{4.04} t\,dt = -96.04\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{4.04}= -96.04\cdot\frac{(4.04)^{2}}{2}\approx -96.04\cdot8.16\approx -784\,$J.
The negative sign indicates work done by gravity is in the direction of motion; magnitude $784\,$J.

practice.q: A spring obeys Hooke’s law with constant $k=200\,$N/m. It is compressed 0.1 m and then released. Find the total mechanical energy stored in the spring and the maximum speed of a 0.5 kg block attached to it.
practice.a:
Elastic potential energy $U=\frac12 kx^{2}=\frac12(200)(0.1)^{2}= \frac12(200)(0.01)=1\,$J.
All this energy converts to kinetic energy at the equilibrium point: $K=\frac12 mv_{\max }^{2}=U$.
Solve for $v_{\max }$: $\frac12(0.5)v_{\max }^{2}=1\Rightarrow 0.25 v_{\max }^{2}=1\Rightarrow v_{\max }^{2}=4\Rightarrow v_{\max }=2\,$m/s.

practice.q: A particle moves along the $x$‑axis with acceleration $a(t)=6t-4$ m/s², where $t$ is in seconds. At $t=0$, its position is $x(0)=2\,$m and its velocity is $v(0)=3\,$m/s. (a) Find the position function $x(t)$. (b) Compute the work done by the net force from $t=0$ to $t=5\,$s. (Assume mass $m=2\,$kg.)

A water tank has a cross‑sectional area $A=2\,$m². Water flows in at a rate $Q_{\text{in}}(t)=5+0.5t$ m³/min and out at a rate $Q_{\text{out}}(t)=3+0.2t^{2}$ m³/min. The tank initially contains $V(0)=10\,$m³ of water. (a) Write a differential equation for the volume $V(t)$. (b) Find $V(t)$ for $0\le t\le 4$ minutes. (c) Compute the work required to pump all the water out of the tank at $t=4$ min, assuming the water surface is at height $h(t)=V(t)/A$ and the pump lifts water to a height of $5\,$m above the tank. (Take $g=9.8\,$m/s², density $\rho=1000\,$kg/m³.)
practice.a:
(a) Rate of change of volume equals inflow minus outflow:
$\displaystyle \frac{dV}{dt}=Q_{\text{in}}(t)-Q_{\text{out}}(t)=\big(5+0.5t\big)-\big(3+0.2t^{2}\big)=2+0.5t-0.2t^{2}$.
(b) Integrate from $0$ to $t$:
$V(t)=V(0)+\int_{0}^{t}\big(2+0.5\tau-0.2\tau^{2}\big)d\tau$
$=10+\Big[2\tau+\frac{0.5}{2}\tau^{2}-\frac{0.2}{3}\tau^{3}\Big]_{0}^{t}$
$=10+2t+0.25t^{2}-\frac{0.2}{3}t^{3}$.
For $t=4$:
$V(4)=10+2(4)+0.25(16)-\frac{0.2}{3}(64)$
$=10+8+4- \frac{12.8}{3}$
$=22-4.267\approx17.733\,$m³.
(c) At any time $t$, water height $h(t)=V(t)/A$. The infinitesimal mass $dm=\rho\,dV$ is lifted a distance $d=5-h(t)$. Work $dW= g\,dm\,d = g\rho\,(5-h(t))\,dV$.
Total work from $t=0$ to $4$ is
$W=g\rho\int_{0}^{4}\big(5-\frac{V(t)}{A}\big)\frac{dV}{dt}\,dt$.
But $\frac{dV}{dt}=2+0.5t-0.2t^{2}$ and $V(t)=10+2t+0.25t^{2}-\frac{0.2}{3}t^{3}$.
Compute integrand:
$5-\frac{V(t)}{2}=5-\frac{1}{2}\big(10+2t+0.25t^{2}-\frac{0.2}{3}t^{3}\big)$
$=5-\big(5+t+0.125t^{2}-\frac{0.1}{3}t^{3}\big)$
$= -t-0.125t^{2}+ \frac{0.1}{3}t^{3}$.
Thus
$W= g\rho\int_{0}^{4}\big(-t-0.125t^{2}+ \frac{0.1}{3}t^{3}\big)\big(2+0.5t-0.2t^{2}\big)dt$.
Expand the product (omitting algebraic steps for brevity) to obtain a polynomial $P(t)$. After expansion and integration:
$P(t)= -2t -0.25t^{2}+0.2t^{3} -0.25t^{2}-0.0625t^{3}+0.05t^{4}+ \frac{0.2}{3}t^{3}+ \frac{0.05}{3}t^{4}-\frac{0.02}{3}t^{5}$
Combine like terms:
$P(t)= -2t -0.5t^{2}+ \big(0.2-0.0625+\frac{0.2}{3}\big)t^{3}+ \big(0.05+\frac{0.05}{3}\big)t^{4}-\frac{0.02}{3}t^{5}$
Compute coefficients:
$t^{3}$: $0.2-0.0625+0.0667\approx0.2042$
$t^{4}$: $0.05+0.0167=0.0667$
So $P(t)\approx -2t -0.5t^{2}+0.204t^{3}+0.0667t^{4}-0.00667t^{5}$.
Now integrate from $0$ to $4$:
$\int P(t)dt = -t^{2} -\frac{0.5}{3}t^{3}+ \frac{0.204}{4}t^{4}+ \frac{0.0667}{5}t^{5}-\frac{0.00667}{6}t^{6}\Big|_{0}^{4}$
Evaluate at $t=4$:
$-16 -\frac{0.5}{3}(64)+0.051t^{4}(256)+0.01334t^{5}(1024)-0.001112t^{6}(4096)$
Compute each term:
$-16$
$-\frac{0.5}{3}\cdot64 = -\frac{32}{3}\approx -10.667$
$0.051\cdot256\approx13.056$
$0.01334\cdot1024\approx13.658$
$-0.001112\cdot4096\approx -4.556$
Sum: $-16-10.667+13.056+13.658-4.556\approx -4.509$.
Thus $\int_{0}^{4}P(t)dt\approx -4.51\,$m³·m (the negative sign indicates the pump does work against gravity).
Finally $W = g\rho \times | -4.51| = 9.8 \times 1000 \times 4.51\approx 44\,200\,$J.
So about $4.4\times10^{4}$ joules of work are required.

data.recap: This lesson connects calculus tools to physics problems. It reviews how limits give instantaneous rates, how derivatives turn position into velocity and acceleration, and how definite integrals calculate work. The steps for solving real‑world problems combine limits, derivatives, and integrals, and the lesson stresses checking units and intuition. Practice problems reinforce these ideas.

key_terms.meaning: The limit of average change as the time interval shrinks to zero, also called the derivative.
A function that gives the instantaneous rate of change of another function with respect to its variable.
The derivative of position with respect to time; it tells how fast and in what direction an object moves at an instant.
The derivative of velocity with respect to time, or the second derivative of position.
The sum of infinitely many tiny contributions, used to calculate total quantities like work or distance.
The integral of the force component along the direction of motion over a displacement.
Verifying that the units of a calculated answer match the expected physical units.
A line that touches a curve at a single point and has the same slope as the curve there; its slope equals the instantaneous rate of change.

quiz.q: What does the limit definition of the derivative represent in physics?
options: Average speed over a long time
quiz.why: It gives the exact rate at a single instant, which is the definition of instantaneous rate of change.

quiz.q: If s(t) = 5t^2, what is the velocity v(t)?
quiz.why: Velocity is the derivative of position: d/dt of 5t^2 is 10t.

quiz.q: Which expression correctly represents work done by a variable force F(x) from x_i to x_f?
options: integral of F(x) dx from x_i to x_f
quiz.why: Work is the definite integral of force over displacement.

quiz.q: What are the units of acceleration?
quiz.why: Acceleration is change in velocity (m/s) per time (s), giving m/s^2.

quiz.q: Why is checking the sign of an answer important in physics problems?
options: It confirms the calculation was done quickly
It ensures the direction of the quantity matches the physical situation
It makes the answer look nicer
quiz.why: The sign indicates direction, which must agree with the problem’s context.

quiz.q: In a car problem where force F(v)=F0 - k*v, which calculus tool helps find the distance traveled over time?
options: A combination of limits, derivatives, and integrals
quiz.why: All three tools are needed: limits for instantaneous velocity, derivatives for acceleration, and integrals to sum distance.

flashcards.front: What is the instantaneous rate of change?
flashcards.back: It is the limit of the average change as the interval approaches zero; mathematically, the derivative.

flashcards.front: How do you obtain velocity from a position function?
flashcards.back: Take the derivative of the position function with respect to time.

flashcards.front: What does a definite integral compute in physics?
flashcards.back: It adds up tiny contributions, such as work from a variable force or total distance from speed.

flashcards.front: State the definition of work in terms of an integral.
flashcards.back: Work equals the integral of the force component along the motion direction over the displacement interval.

flashcards.front: Why check units in a physics answer?
flashcards.back: Units verify that the calculation matches the physical quantity being asked for.

flashcards.front: What is the physical meaning of the tangent line to a position-time curve?
flashcards.back: Its slope equals the instantaneous velocity at that point.

flashcards.front: How is acceleration related to position?
flashcards.back: Acceleration is the second derivative of position with respect to time.

flashcards.front: What step ensures a physics solution makes sense beyond the math?
flashcards.back: Compare the sign, magnitude, and units with real‑world intuition.

data.title: biology
data.summary: This lesson shows how calculus concepts—limits, derivatives, and integrals—are applied to biological problems. Students will see concrete examples such as population growth, enzyme kinetics, and drug dosage modeling.
objectives: Explain how a limit describes a biological process approaching a steady state
Compute the derivative of a population growth function and interpret its meaning
Set up and evaluate a definite integral to find total biomass or drug amount over time
Model a simple biological system using differential equations and solve it
Critically assess the assumptions behind each calculus model in biology
data.prerequisites: Students should already understand basic limits, derivatives, and definite integrals from earlier lessons.
why: Biology often deals with change—how populations grow, how concentrations vary, and how organisms respond over time. Calculus provides the language and tools to quantify these changes, turning qualitative observations into precise predictions.

Real‑world applications include managing wildlife populations, designing effective drug dosing schedules, and understanding how ecosystems respond to environmental stress. Mastering these models prepares students for careers in health, ecology, and biotechnology.

sections.heading: 1. Limits in Biological Contexts
sections.body:
Imagine you are watching a small dish of bacteria growing in a lab. At first the number of cells rises quickly, then it seems to slow down, and finally it stops changing much at all.  The idea of a **limit** helps us describe exactly what is happening when the growth “gets close” to a final value, even if the bacteria never quite reach it.

> **Definition:** A limit describes the value that a quantity *approaches* as the input gets nearer and nearer to a certain point.  
> In symbols we write  
> $$\lim_{t\to\infty} N(t)=K,$$  
> meaning “as time $t$ becomes larger and larger, the population $N(t)$ gets closer and closer to the number $K$.”

---

### Why limits matter in biology  

Biologists often work with processes that never finish in a single instant.  A population might keep changing for years, a drug concentration might keep decreasing forever, or a chemical reaction might keep approaching equilibrium.  Limits give us a precise way to talk about the *long‑term* behaviour of these processes without having to wait forever.

Think of a ball rolling down a hill that eventually comes to rest at the bottom.  The ball’s speed is never exactly zero while it is moving, but we can say that the speed *approaches* zero as time goes on.  The same idea works for a bacterial culture: the number of cells $N(t)$ approaches a maximum size, called the **carrying capacity** $K$, as time $t$ grows.

---

### A concrete example: logistic growth  

A simple model for bacterial growth is the logistic equation  

$$\frac{dN}{dt}=rN\Bigl(1-\frac{N}{K}\Bigr),$$  

where  

* $N(t)$ = number of bacteria at time $t$,  
* $r$ = intrinsic growth rate (how fast the bacteria would grow if there were no limits),  
* $K$ = carrying capacity (the largest population the environment can sustain).

If we solve this differential equation (we will do that later in the course), we obtain  

$$N(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ce^{-rt}},$$  

with $C$ a constant determined by the initial population.  Look at what happens when $t$ becomes very large:

$$\lim_{t\to\infty} N(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ce^{-\infty}}=\frac{K}{1+0}=K.$$

So the limit tells us that, no matter how many bacteria we start with (as long as it is positive), the population will get ever closer to $K$ and will never exceed it.

> **In daily life:** Think of a bathtub filling with water.  The water level rises quickly at first, then slows as the faucet is turned off, and finally the level approaches the rim of the tub.  The height of the water has a limit – the rim height – even though the water never actually spills over.

---

### How to read a limit statement  

1. **Identify the variable that is changing** – here it is time $t$.  
2. **Identify the direction** – $t\to\infty$ means “as $t$ gets larger without bound.”  
3. **Identify the expression** – $N(t)$ is the quantity we watch.  
4. **Identify the limiting value** – $K$ is the number we expect $N(t)$ to approach.

If any of these parts are unclear, the whole statement can be confusing.  Always ask: *What is changing? What is it changing toward? What is the target value?*

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that the limit value is actually reached.  In the logistic example, $N(t)$ gets arbitrarily close to $K$, but it never becomes exactly $K$ at any finite time.  Limits describe “approach,” not “arrival.”

---

### Why you should remember this  

Limits give us a language for talking about steady‑state situations – the points where a biological system stops changing in a noticeable way.  Later we will use limits to define derivatives (instantaneous rates) and integrals (total accumulated amounts).  Mastering the basic idea now will make those later concepts much easier.

> **Remember:** A limit is about *approaching* a value, not necessarily *reaching* it.  It lets us capture the long‑term trend of a biological process in a single, precise statement.

sections.heading: 2. Derivatives as Rates of Change
sections.body:
The word **derivative** means “how fast something is changing at a single instant.”  
Imagine you are watching a video of a growing bacterial colony. At each frame you can see the number of cells, but the frames are spaced a little apart. The derivative tells us what would happen **between** the frames – the exact speed of growth at any precise moment.

> **Definition:** The derivative of a function $f(t)$ with respect to time $t$, written $f'(t)$ or $\displaystyle\frac{df}{dt}$, is the limit of the average change $\dfrac{f(t+\Delta t)-f(t)}{\Delta t}$ as the time interval $\Delta t$ becomes infinitely small.

Why is this useful? In biology we often need the *instantaneous* growth rate of a population, the *speed* of an enzyme reaction, or the *rate* at which a drug leaves the bloodstream. Knowing the derivative lets us predict what will happen a tiny moment later, which is essential for planning experiments or treatments.

---

### Example 1: Exponential population growth  

A simple model for a population that reproduces without limits is  

$$P(t)=P_0 e^{rt},$$  

where  

* $P(t)$ = number of individuals at time $t$,  
* $P_0$ = initial population size,  
* $r$ = constant per‑capita growth rate (per day, per hour, …),  
* $e$ = the base of natural logarithms (≈ 2.718).

To find the instantaneous growth rate, differentiate $P(t)$ with respect to $t$.

1. Write the function: $P(t)=P_0 e^{rt}$.  
2. Recall the rule: $\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}e^{rt}=r e^{rt}$ (the exponent comes down as a factor).  
3. Apply the rule:

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=P_0 \, r e^{rt}.$$

4. Notice that $P_0 e^{rt}=P(t)$, so we can rewrite

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=r\,P(t).$$

Interpretation: the instantaneous growth rate at any time is the constant $r$ multiplied by the current population size. If $r=0.05\ \text{day}^{-1}$ and $P(t)=200$, then $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.05\times200=10$ individuals per day at that exact moment.

> **In daily life:** This is like a bank account that earns interest continuously. The derivative tells you how much money is added *right now*, not just after a month.

---

### Example 2: Speed of an enzyme‑catalyzed reaction  

The Michaelis–Menten equation gives the reaction rate $v$ (amount of product formed per unit time) as a function of substrate concentration $[S]$:

$$v([S])=\frac{V_{\max}[S]}{K_m+[S]},$$  

where  

* $V_{\max}$ = maximum possible rate,  
* $K_m$ = substrate concentration at which the rate is half of $V_{\max}$.

Suppose the substrate concentration changes over time, $[S]=[S](t)$. To find how fast the rate itself is changing, differentiate $v$ with respect to $t$ using the chain rule.

1. Write $v$ as a function of $[S]$: $v([S])=\dfrac{V_{\max}[S]}{K_m+[S]}$.  
2. Differentiate with respect to $t$:

$$\frac{dv}{dt}= \frac{d v}{d [S]}\,\frac{d [S]}{dt}.$$

3. Compute $\displaystyle\frac{d v}{d [S]}$ using the quotient rule  
   $\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}\frac{u}{w}= \frac{u' w - u w'}{w^2}$ with $u=V_{\max}[S]$, $w=K_m+[S]$:

\[
\frac{d v}{d [S]} = \frac{V_{\max}(K_m+[S]) - V_{\max}[S](1)}{(K_m+[S])^{2}}
= \frac{V_{\max}K_m}{(K_m+[S])^{2}}.
\]

4. Multiply by $\displaystyle\frac{d [S]}{dt}$ (the change of substrate concentration):

$$\frac{dv}{dt}= \frac{V_{\max}K_m}{(K_m+[S])^{2}}\,\frac{d [S]}{dt}.$$

Interpretation: if the substrate is being consumed ($\frac{d[S]}{dt}<0$), the reaction rate will also decrease, and the factor $\frac{V_{\max}K_m}{(K_m+[S])^{2}}$ tells us how sensitive the rate is to that change at the current concentration.

> **Note:** The chain rule is the key idea here – you first find how the output changes with the input, then multiply by how the input changes with time.

---

### Putting it together  

The derivative converts a *change over an interval* into a *change at a point*. In biology, this lets us:

* Predict the number of new cells that will appear in the next minute, not just after an hour.  
* Adjust drug dosage by knowing how quickly the drug concentration is falling at any moment.  
* Understand how a sudden drop in substrate (e.g., glucose) will instantly slow down an enzyme’s activity.

> **Remember:** Always check the units. If $P(t)$ is in individuals and $t$ is in days, then $dP/dt$ is “individuals per day.” Matching units helps avoid the common mistake of mixing rates with totals.

With these ideas, you can move from a static picture of a biological system to a dynamic one that tells you exactly how fast things are happening right now.

sections.heading: 3. Modeling Population Growth
sections.body:
Population growth is a classic example where calculus helps us turn a simple idea – “the more individuals there are, the faster the population can increase” – into a precise mathematical model.

> **Definition:** *Model* – a mathematical description that captures the essential behavior of a real‑world situation, allowing us to make predictions or understand patterns.

### 1. The exponential growth model  

Imagine a colony of bacteria that doubles every hour. If we start with $P_0$ bacteria at time $t=0$, after one hour we have $2P_0$, after two hours $4P_0$, and so on. The pattern is that the population at time $t$ is multiplied by a constant factor each unit of time.

We translate this idea into a rate statement: the **instantaneous rate of change** of the population, denoted $\frac{dP}{dt}$, is proportional to the current size $P(t)$. The word *proportional* means there is a constant $r$ such that  

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=r\,P(t).$$  

Here $r$ is called the **intrinsic growth rate**; it tells how fast the population would grow if it were very small. A positive $r$ means growth, a negative $r$ would mean decline.

To find $P(t)$ we solve the differential equation. Separate the variables:

$$\frac{1}{P}\,dP = r\,dt.$$

Integrate both sides:

$$\int \frac{1}{P}\,dP = \int r\,dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln|P| = rt + C,$$

where $C$ is the constant of integration. Exponentiate to remove the logarithm:

$$P(t)=e^{rt+C}=e^{C}\,e^{rt}.$$

Since $e^{C}$ is just another constant, we rename it $P_0$, the initial population at $t=0$. The final formula is  

$$\boxed{P(t)=P_0\,e^{rt}}.$$

**Interpretation of parameters**

- $P_0$: the number of individuals at the start of observation.  
- $r$: how quickly each individual contributes to new individuals (per unit time).  
- $e^{rt}$: the factor by which the population has multiplied after time $t$.

> **In daily life:** Exponential growth describes unchecked spread of a rumor, the compound interest on a bank account, or the early phase of an epidemic when few people are immune.

### 2. The logistic growth model  

Exponential growth cannot continue forever; resources such as food, space, or light become limited. To capture this, we introduce a **carrying capacity** $K$, the maximum population that the environment can sustain.

The idea is that the growth rate should slow down as $P(t)$ approaches $K$. A simple way to express this is  

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=r\,P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).$$  

The new factor $\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$ is called the **limiting factor**. When $P$ is much smaller than $K$, the term is close to 1 and the equation reduces to the exponential case. When $P$ gets near $K$, the term approaches 0, making the growth rate tiny.

Again we separate variables:

$$\frac{dP}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)} = r\,dt.$$

Using partial fractions,  

$$\frac{1}{P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)} = \frac{1}{P} + \frac{1}{K-P}\,\frac{1}{K}.$$

Integrating gives  

$$\ln|P| - \ln|K-P| = rt + C.$$

Combine the logarithms:

$$\ln\!\left(\frac{P}{K-P}\right)=rt + C.$$

Exponentiate:

$$\frac{P}{K-P}=Ce^{rt}.$$

Solve for $P$:

$$P(t)=\frac{K\,Ce^{rt}}{1+Ce^{rt}}.$$

We determine $C$ from the initial condition $P(0)=P_0$:

$$\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}=C.$$

Substituting back yields the classic logistic formula  

$$\boxed{P(t)=\frac{K}{1+\left(\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}}.$$

**Interpretation of parameters**

- $K$: the environmental ceiling; no matter how long we wait, $P(t)$ cannot exceed $K$.  
- $r$: still the intrinsic growth rate, governing how quickly the population moves toward $K$.  
- The fraction $\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}$ measures how far the starting population is from the ceiling; a small $P_0$ makes this fraction large, leading to a slower early rise.

> **Note:** The logistic curve starts looking like an exponential curve, then bends and levels off, forming an “S‑shape” (sigmoid).

### 3. Why these models matter  

Both formulas let us predict future population sizes, compare different species, or evaluate the impact of conservation measures. By fitting real data to the equations, we can estimate $r$ and $K$, gaining insight into how fast a species reproduces and how much habitat it needs.

> **Remember:** Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources; logistic growth adds a realistic cap through the carrying capacity $K$. Using the wrong model can lead to wildly inaccurate forecasts.

sections.heading: 4. Integrals for Accumulated Quantities
sections.body:
Imagine you have a garden and you measure how fast the plants are growing each day.  
The number you get each day is a **rate** – for example, “the garden gains 2 kg of biomass per day”.  
If you add up all those tiny daily gains over a whole month, you obtain the **total** amount of new biomass.  

> **Definition:** A *definite integral* is the mathematical tool that adds up (accumulates) a continuously changing quantity over an interval of time or space.  

In symbols, if $f(t)$ tells us the instantaneous rate of change at time $t$, then the total change from time $a$ to time $b$ is written  

$$
\int_{a}^{b} f(t)\,dt .
$$  

The little “$dt$” means “a very small piece of time”. Multiplying the rate $f(t)$ by a tiny time slice $dt$ gives a tiny amount of the quantity, and the integral adds all those tiny pieces together.

### Why does this work?

Think of a river. The water flow at any moment is measured in cubic meters per second, say $Q(t)$. To find how many cubic meters pass a point in one hour, you could record the flow every second and add the numbers. The integral does exactly that, but it uses infinitely many infinitesimally small slices, giving a precise total without having to count each second.

### A simple biological example

Suppose a bacterial culture grows at a rate that changes with time:  

$$
r(t)=3+0.5t \quad\text{(grams per hour)},
$$  

where $t$ is measured in hours after the experiment starts.  
We want the total biomass produced between $t=0$ and $t=4$ h.

1. **Write the integral**  

   $$
   \text{Total biomass}= \int_{0}^{4} (3+0.5t)\,dt .
   $$

2. **Find an antiderivative** – a function whose derivative is the integrand.  
   The antiderivative of $3$ is $3t$, and the antiderivative of $0.5t$ is $0.5\cdot\frac{t^{2}}{2}=0.25t^{2}$.  
   So one antiderivative is  

   $$
   F(t)=3t+0.25t^{2}.
   $$

3. **Evaluate at the limits**  

   $$
   \int_{0}^{4} (3+0.5t)\,dt = F(4)-F(0)
   =\bigl(3\cdot4+0.25\cdot4^{2}\bigr)-\bigl(3\cdot0+0.25\cdot0^{2}\bigr)
   =12+4-0=16\ \text{grams}.
   $$  

So the culture adds **16 g** of biomass in the first four hours.

> **In daily life:** Adding up the amount of water that flows from a faucet each minute gives the total water used during a shower. The integral does the same thing when the flow changes continuously.

### Another example: drug delivery

A medication is infused into a patient at a rate that slowly decreases as the pump runs down:  

$$
d(t)=5e^{-0.2t}\quad\text{(milligrams per hour)}.
$$  

How much drug enters the bloodstream in the first 3 hours?

1. Set up the integral  

   $$
   \int_{0}^{3} 5e^{-0.2t}\,dt .
   $$

2. Antiderivative: the integral of $e^{kt}$ is $\frac{1}{k}e^{kt}$. Here $k=-0.2$, so  

   $$
   F(t)=5\left(\frac{1}{-0.2}\right)e^{-0.2t}= -25e^{-0.2t}.
   $$

3. Evaluate  

   $$
   -25e^{-0.2\cdot3}+25e^{-0.2\cdot0}
   =-25e^{-0.6}+25
   \approx -25(0.549)+25
   \approx -13.73+25 = 11.27\ \text{mg}.
   $$  

Thus about **11.3 mg** of the drug is delivered in the first three hours.

> **Note:** The integral gives the exact total even when the rate is not constant. You do not need to measure every tiny interval; the formula does the work for you.

### Key ideas to remember

- The **integrand** $f(t)$ is the rate you are adding up.  
- The **limits** $a$ and $b$ tell you the start and end of the interval.  
- Finding an **antiderivative** (also called a *primitive*) lets you evaluate the integral quickly using the **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus**:  

  $$
  \int_{a}^{b} f(t)\,dt = F(b)-F(a),
  $$  

  where $F'(t)=f(t)$.

> **Remember:** A definite integral is not a mysterious new object; it is simply “adding up a changing amount” over a period. Whenever you see a rate (growth, flow, dosage), the integral tells you the total amount accumulated.

sections.heading: 5. Solving a Simple Differential Equation
sections.body:
We want to understand how a simple differential equation can describe a growing population and how to solve it step by step.

First, imagine a small pond that already has some fish. If we look at the pond after a short time, we notice that the number of new fish that appear is roughly proportional to how many fish are already there – more fish means more babies. This idea is captured by a **first‑order differential equation**.  

> **Definition:** A *differential equation* is an equation that relates a function (here the population size) to its derivative (its rate of change). A *first‑order* equation involves only the first derivative.

Let $P(t)$ be the number of individuals at time $t$ (measured in days, weeks, etc.). The statement “the growth rate is proportional to the current population” translates to  

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=k\,P,$$

where $k$ is a constant called the *growth constant*. If $k>0$, the population grows; if $k<0$, it shrinks.  

> **Note:** The symbol $\frac{dP}{dt}$ reads “the derivative of $P$ with respect to $t$” and means “how fast $P$ is changing at that moment”.

### Solving by separation of variables

The equation $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$ can be rearranged so that all $P$‑terms are on one side and all $t$‑terms on the other. This technique is called *separation of variables*.

1. Divide both sides by $P$ (assuming $P\neq0$) and multiply by $dt$:

$$\frac{1}{P}\,dP = k\,dt.$$

2. Now each side involves only one variable, so we can integrate (find the antiderivative) of both sides:

$$\int \frac{1}{P}\,dP = \int k\,dt.$$

3. The integrals are straightforward:

$$\ln|P| = k t + C,$$

where $\ln$ is the natural logarithm, $|P|$ denotes absolute value (populations are positive, so we can drop the bars later), and $C$ is the *constant of integration* that appears because we do not know the exact starting point yet.

4. Solve for $P$ by exponentiating both sides. Remember that $e^{\ln x}=x$:

$$|P| = e^{k t + C}=e^{C}\,e^{k t}.$$

Since $P$ is positive, we drop the absolute value and write $e^{C}$ as a new constant $P_0$ (the population at time $t=0$):

$$P(t)=P_0\,e^{k t}.$$

This is the famous *exponential growth formula*.

### Verifying the solution

To be sure our solution works, we can differentiate $P(t)$ and check that it satisfies the original equation.

Take the derivative of $P(t)=P_0 e^{k t}$:

$$\frac{dP}{dt}=P_0\,k\,e^{k t}=k\,P_0 e^{k t}=k\,P(t).$$

We see that $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$, exactly the equation we started with, so the solution is correct.

> **In daily life:** This same math describes how a bank account grows when interest is added continuously. The balance $B(t)$ follows $\frac{dB}{dt}=rB$, giving $B(t)=B_0 e^{rt}$.

### Putting numbers to the model

Suppose a colony of bacteria starts with $P_0=100$ cells and doubles every hour. Doubling means $P(1)=2P_0$, so

$$2P_0 = P_0 e^{k\cdot1}\quad\Rightarrow\quad e^{k}=2\quad\Rightarrow\quad k=\ln 2\approx0.693.$$

The model becomes

$$P(t)=100\,e^{0.693\,t}.$$

If we want the population after 3.5 hours, plug $t=3.5$:

$$P(3.5)=100\,e^{0.693\times3.5}\approx100\,e^{2.425}\approx100\times11.3\approx1130\text{ cells}.$$

> **Remember:** Always check the units of $k$ and $t$ so they match (e.g., $k$ per hour if $t$ is in hours).

### Common pitfalls

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to add the constant $C$ after integration. Without $C$, you would incorrectly force the solution to pass through the origin, which is rarely true for real populations.

By separating variables, integrating, and then verifying, we have turned a simple biological observation into a precise mathematical prediction. This process is the foundation for many more complex models in biology, chemistry, and economics.

sections.heading: 6. Application: Drug Dosage Over Time
sections.body:
When a patient takes a single dose of a medicine, the amount of drug in the bloodstream does not stay constant.  
First the concentration rises as the drug is absorbed, then it falls because the body breaks it down and removes it.  
We can describe this behaviour with a simple **decay function** and use calculus to answer two practical questions:

* At what time is the concentration highest (the *peak*)?  
* How much total drug exposure does the body receive over a certain period?

---

**Idea in plain words**  
Imagine you pour a cup of water into a bathtub that already has water flowing out through a drain.  
The water level first goes up (the inflow) and then goes down (the outflow).  
If we know the rate at which water leaves, we can predict the level at any later time.  
In pharmacology the “water level” is the drug concentration $C(t)$ (amount per litre of blood) and the “drain” is the body’s elimination process.

---

### 1.  A simple decay model

For many drugs the elimination follows **first‑order kinetics**: the rate at which the drug leaves the body is proportional to the amount currently present.  
Mathematically this means

$$\frac{dC}{dt} = -k\,C(t),$$

where  

* $C(t)$ = concentration at time $t$ (hours after the dose),  
* $k>0$ = **elimination constant** (per hour), and  
* $\frac{dC}{dt}$ = derivative of $C$, i.e., the instantaneous rate of change of concentration.

> **Definition:** *First‑order kinetics* means the change per unit time depends linearly on the current amount.

Solving the differential equation gives the familiar exponential decay formula

$$C(t)=C_0\,e^{-k t},$$

where $C_0$ is the concentration right after the drug has been fully absorbed (the **initial concentration**).

> **Note:** The exponential function $e^{x}$ grows very fast for positive $x$ and shrinks quickly for negative $x$. Here the exponent is negative, so the function decreases.

---

### 2.  Finding the peak concentration

In reality the drug is not instantaneously absorbed; it enters the bloodstream over a short period.  
A common way to model this is to add a **input term** $R(t)$ that represents the rate at which the drug enters the blood.  
A simple choice is a constant infusion for a short time $T_{\text{inf}}$:

$$R(t)=\begin{cases}
R_0, & 0\le t\le T_{\text{inf}},\\[4pt]
0,   & t> T_{\text{inf}}.
\end{cases}$$

Now the governing equation becomes

$$\frac{dC}{dt}=R(t)-k\,C(t).$$

During the infusion ($0\le t\le T_{\text{inf}}$) we have

$$\frac{dC}{dt}=R_0-k\,C(t).$$

This is a linear differential equation whose solution is

$$C(t)=\frac{R_0}{k}\Bigl(1-e^{-k t}\Bigr).$$

The concentration rises from $0$ toward the **steady‑state value** $R_0/k$.  
The peak occurs at the end of the infusion, because after $t=T_{\text{inf}}$ the input stops and the derivative becomes negative:

$$C_{\text{peak}} = C(T_{\text{inf}})=\frac{R_0}{k}\Bigl(1-e^{-k T_{\text{inf}}}\Bigr).$$

> **In daily life:** Think of filling a bathtub while the drain is open. The water level climbs while you keep the tap on, then starts to fall as soon as you turn the tap off.

---

### 3.  Total drug exposure (area under the curve)

Doctors often talk about the **AUC** – *area under the concentration‑time curve* – because it measures the total amount of drug that the body experiences.  
Mathematically, the AUC from time $0$ to some later time $T$ is the integral of $C(t)$:

$$\text{AUC}(0,T)=\int_{0}^{T} C(t)\,dt.$$

Using the decay formula after the infusion ends ($t>T_{\text{inf}}$), the concentration follows $C(t)=C_{\text{peak}}e^{-k(t-T_{\text{inf}})}$.  
Integrating from $T_{\text{inf}}$ to infinity gives the total exposure after the dose:

$$\text{AUC}= \int_{0}^{T_{\text{inf}}}\frac{R_0}{k}\bigl(1-e^{-k t}\bigr)dt
          +\int_{T_{\text{inf}}}^{\infty} C_{\text{peak}}e^{-k(t-T_{\text{inf}})}dt.$$

Carrying out the integrals (the antiderivative of $e^{-k t}$ is $-\frac{1}{k}e^{-k t}$) yields

$$\text{AUC}= \frac{R_0}{k}T_{\text{inf}}-\frac{R_0}{k^{2}}\bigl(1-e^{-k T_{\text{inf}}}\bigr)
            +\frac{C_{\text{peak}}}{k}.$$

Because $C_{\text{peak}}=\frac{R_0}{k}\bigl(1-e^{-k T_{\text{inf}}}\bigr)$, the two middle terms cancel, leaving the simple result

$$\boxed{\text{AUC}= \frac{R_0}{k}\,T_{\text{inf}}+\frac{R_0}{k^{2}}\bigl(1-e^{-k T_{\text{inf}}}\bigr)}.$$

> **Remember:** The AUC combines both how high the concentration gets and how long it stays there. A larger AUC means more overall drug effect (or risk of side effects).

---

### 4.  Why this matters

* **Dosing schedules** – By adjusting $R_0$ (dose size) or $T_{\text{inf}}$ (how fast the drug is given), clinicians can control $C_{\text{peak}}$ and the AUC, tailoring treatment to the patient’s needs.  
* **Safety** – Knowing the peak helps avoid concentrations that could be toxic, while the AUC helps ensure the drug stays effective over the required time.  
* **Comparison** – Different drugs with the same AUC may have very different peaks; calculus lets us see both aspects clearly.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that after the infusion stops, the concentration still changes (it decays). Ignoring the decay part would over‑estimate the peak and the AUC.

sections.heading: 7. Limitations and Model Critique
sections.body:
When we write a mathematical model for a biological system we are really making a *story* about how the system works.  
Every story needs characters, a setting, and a plot. In a population‑growth model the characters are the individuals, the setting is the environment (food, temperature, predators, …), and the plot is the rule that tells us how the number of individuals changes over time.  

If the story is too simple, the plot may look nice on paper but it will not match what really happens in nature. Below we look at the most common simplifying assumptions, see how they can bend our results, and suggest ways to make the story richer using more advanced calculus ideas.

> **Note:** *Assumption* means something we decide to treat as fixed or ignore, even though in reality it can change.

### 1. Constant environment  

The classic logistic model  

$$\frac{dN}{dt}=rN\left(1-\frac{N}{K}\right)$$  

assumes that the growth rate $r$ and the carrying capacity $K$ stay the same for all time. In the real world, temperature, rainfall, or the amount of food can vary from day to day, making $r$ and $K$ functions of time: $r(t)$, $K(t)$.  

If we keep $r$ and $K$ constant, the solution $N(t)$ will approach a single steady value $K$. In a season where food is scarce, the true population may drop far below $K$, but our model would still predict a smooth approach to $K$, giving a false sense of stability.

**How to improve:** Replace the constants by *time‑dependent* functions and use the technique of **separation of variables** or **integrating factors** to solve  

$$\frac{dN}{dt}=r(t)N\left(1-\frac{N}{K(t)}\right).$$  

This requires evaluating integrals that may not have a simple closed form, but numerical integration (e.g., the Euler or Runge‑Kutta methods) can give accurate predictions.

### 2. No age structure  

The differential equation above treats every individual as identical, regardless of whether it is a newborn, a mature adult, or an elderly animal. In many species, only adults reproduce, and mortality rates differ by age. Ignoring this leads to over‑ or under‑estimation of growth, especially when a large fraction of the population is young.

**Why it matters:** Suppose a disease kills only juveniles. A model without age classes would predict a modest decline, while the real population could crash because the breeding pool disappears.

**How to improve:** Introduce *structured* models such as the **McKendrick–von Foerster equation**

$$\frac{\partial n(a,t)}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial n(a,t)}{\partial a}=-\mu(a)n(a,t),$$  

where $n(a,t)$ is the density of individuals of age $a$ at time $t$, and $\mu(a)$ is the age‑specific mortality rate. Solving this partial differential equation (PDE) often involves the method of characteristics, a calculus tool that follows the path of an individual through age and time.

### 3. Ignoring stochastic events  

Deterministic models give a single, smooth curve for $N(t)$. Real populations experience random events: sudden weather changes, accidental introductions of predators, or random births and deaths. These *stochastic* effects can cause extinction even when the deterministic model predicts persistence.

**Everyday comparison:** Think of flipping a fair coin many times. The expected number of heads is $50\%$, but any single series of flips can deviate a lot from that average. Similarly, a population can deviate from its expected growth path.

**How to improve:** Add a random term to the differential equation, forming a **stochastic differential equation (SDE)**  

$$dN = rN\left(1-\frac{N}{K}\right)dt + \sigma N\,dW_t,$$  

where $dW_t$ represents a small random “wiggle” (Brownian motion) and $\sigma$ measures its strength. Solving SDEs uses Itô calculus, an extension of ordinary calculus that handles randomness.

> **Remember:** Adding realism usually makes the math harder, but modern computers let us explore these richer models without solving everything by hand.

### 4. Summary of the impact  

| Simplifying assumption | Typical effect on predictions | More realistic alternative |
|------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Constant $r$, $K$      | Misses seasonal booms/crashes | $r(t)$, $K(t)$ with time‑varying functions |
| No age structure       | Treats all individuals alike | Age‑structured PDEs (McKendrick–von Foerster) |
| Deterministic only     | Ignores random shocks        | Stochastic differential equations |

By recognizing these assumptions, we can decide when a simple model is enough (e.g., a quick classroom illustration) and when we need the extra calculus tools—variable‑coefficient ODEs, PDEs, or Itô calculus—to capture the true dynamics of living systems.

examples.title: Rate of Enzyme Reaction
examples.given: The concentration $C(t)$ (µM) of product in an enzyme reaction is $C(t)=4t^2+2t+1$. Find the instantaneous rate of product formation at $t=3\,$s.

steps.label: Differentiate $C(t)$
steps.text: Compute $C'(t)=\frac{d}{dt}(4t^2+2t+1)=8t+2$ to get the rate function.

examples.answer: The instantaneous rate at $t=3\,$s is $26\;\mu\text{M/s}$.

examples.title: Drug Dosage with First‑Order Elimination
examples.given: A drug is administered intravenously with an initial concentration $D_0=200\,$mg/L. The body eliminates the drug at a rate proportional to its current concentration: $\displaystyle\frac{dD}{dt}=-kD$, with elimination constant $k=0.15\;\text{h}^{-1}$. Find the concentration after $t=5$ h and the total amount eliminated over the 5 h period.

steps.label: Solve the differential equation
steps.text: Separate variables: $\displaystyle\frac{dD}{D}=-k\,dt$. Integrate: $\ln D = -kt + C$. Exponentiate: $D(t)=C_1e^{-kt}$. Use $D(0)=D_0$ to get $C_1=D_0$, so $D(t)=D_0e^{-kt}$.

examples.answer: After 5 h the drug concentration is $\approx94.5\,$mg/L, and $105.5\,$mg/L has been eliminated.

practice.q: A bacterial culture starts with 200 cells and doubles every hour. Write the exponential growth function $P(t)$ and find the population after 3 hours.
practice.a: The doubling means the growth factor per hour is $2$, so $P(t)=200\\cdot2^{t}$. For $t=3$: $P(3)=200\\cdot2^{3}=200\\cdot8=1600$ cells.

practice.q: The concentration of a drug in the bloodstream follows $C(t)=C_0e^{-0.2t}$, where $C_0=50\\,\\text{mg/L}$. What is the concentration after 5 hours?
practice.a: Plug $t=5$ into the formula: $C(5)=50e^{-0.2\\cdot5}=50e^{-1}=50\\times0.3679\\approx18.4\\,\\text{mg/L}$.

practice.q: A population follows the logistic model $P(t)=\\frac{K}{1+Ae^{-rt}}$ with carrying capacity $K=1000$, growth rate $r=0.3$, and $P(0)=100$. Find $A$ and write $P(t)$.
Solve the differential equation $\\frac{dN}{dt}=0.5N$ with initial condition $N(0)=40$.
practice.a: Separate variables: $\\frac{dN}{N}=0.5\\,dt$. Integrate: $\\ln|N|=0.5t+C$. Exponentiate: $N=e^{0.5t+C}=Ce^{0.5t}$. Use $N(0)=40$: $40=C e^{0}=C$, so $C=40$. Hence $N(t)=40e^{0.5t}$.

practice.q: A drug is administered intravenously at a constant rate $R=10\\,\\text{mg/h}$. It is eliminated from the body with first‑order kinetics $\\frac{dC}{dt}=-kC$, where $k=0.1\\,\\text{h}^{-1}$ and the volume of distribution is $V=5\\,\\text{L}$. Derive the expression for the concentration $C(t)$ and find the steady‑state concentration.
practice.a:
The mass balance for the amount $A(t)=C(t)V$ is
$$\\frac{dA}{dt}=R - kA.$$
Since $A=CV$, $\\frac{d(CV)}{dt}=R - kCV \\Rightarrow V\\frac{dC}{dt}=R - kVC.$
Divide by $V$: $\\frac{dC}{dt}=\\frac{R}{V} - kC.$
This is a linear ODE. Solve using integrating factor $\\mu(t)=e^{kt}$:
$$e^{kt}\\frac{dC}{dt}+ke^{kt}C = \\frac{R}{V}e^{kt} \\Rightarrow \\frac{d}{dt}\\bigl(Ce^{kt}\\bigr)=\\frac{R}{V}e^{kt}.$$
Integrate:
$$Ce^{kt}=\\frac{R}{V}\\int e^{kt}dt + C_0 = \\frac{R}{V}\\frac{e^{kt}}{k}+C_0.$$
Thus
$$C(t)=\\frac{R}{kV}+C_0e^{-kt}.$$
Use $C(0)=0$ (no drug initially) to find $C_0 = -\\frac{R}{kV}$. Hence
$$C(t)=\\frac{R}{kV}\\bigl(1-e^{-kt}\\bigr).$$
Plug numbers: $\\frac{R}{kV}=\\frac{10}{0.1\\times5}=\\frac{10}{0.5}=20\\,\\text{mg/L}$.
So $C(t)=20\\bigl(1-e^{-0.1t}\\bigr)$.
Steady‑state concentration is the limit as $t\\to\\infty$: $C_{ss}=20\\,\\text{mg/L}$.

practice.q: A wildlife reserve models the number of a certain bird species with the differential equation $\\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\\left(1-\\frac{P}{K}\\right)-h$, where $r=0.4\\,\\text{yr}^{-1}$, $K=500$, and a constant harvest $h=30$ birds per year. Find the equilibrium populations and determine which are stable.
practice.a:
Set $\\frac{dP}{dt}=0$:
$$0=0.4P\\left(1-\\frac{P}{500}\\right)-30.$$
Multiply by $10$ to clear the decimal:
$$0=4P\\left(1-\\frac{P}{500}\\right)-300.$$
Expand:
$$0=4P - \\frac{4P^2}{500} - 300 = 4P - \\frac{P^2}{125} - 300.$$
Multiply by $125$:
$$0=500P - P^2 - 37500.$$
Rearrange:
$$P^2 - 500P + 37500 = 0.$$
Solve quadratic:
$$P = \\frac{500 \\pm \\sqrt{500^2 - 4\\cdot37500}}{2}=\\frac{500 \\pm \\sqrt{250000 - 150000}}{2}=\\frac{500 \\pm \\sqrt{100000}}{2}.$$
$$\\sqrt{100000}=316.23.$$
Thus
$$P_1 = \\frac{500 - 316.23}{2}=\\frac{183.77}{2}=91.9,$$
$$P_2 = \\frac{500 + 316.23}{2}=\\frac{816.23}{2}=408.1.$$
Equilibria: $P\\approx 92$ and $P\\approx 408$ birds.
Stability: Compute derivative of RHS, $f(P)=0.4P(1-P/500)-30$.
$$f'(P)=0.4\\left(1-\\frac{P}{500}\\right)+0.4P\\left(-\\frac{1}{500}\\right)=0.4 - \\frac{0.8P}{500}=0.4 - 0.0016P.$$
Evaluate at each equilibrium:
- At $P\\approx 92$: $f'(92)=0.4-0.0016\\times92=0.4-0.1472=0.2528>0$ → unstable (since $f'(P)>0$ gives a repelling equilibrium for 1‑D autonomous ODE).
- At $P\\approx 408$: $f'(408)=0.4-0.0016\\times408=0.4-0.6528=-0.2528<0$ → stable (attracting equilibrium).
Therefore, the low equilibrium (~92 birds) is unstable, and the high equilibrium (~408 birds) is stable.

data.recap: This lesson shows how calculus concepts like limits, derivatives, integrals and differential equations describe biological processes such as population growth, drug concentration, and biomass accumulation. Limits tell us the value a quantity approaches, derivatives give instantaneous rates, integrals add up small changes, and solving differential equations predicts future behavior. The examples connect math to real‑world biology and highlight model assumptions.
